name: The star
title: A light to steer by.
introduction: Long before tarot, a star was something to steer by: the star that led the Magi, and the medieval title of Mary as Stella Maris, star of the sea, to whom sailors prayed. Marseille-pattern decks give The Star a great star ringed by seven smaller ones above a kneeling figure pouring water, and the Waite-Smith card keeps that arrangement. In the Golden Dawn and Waite-Smith lineage the card came to be read as hope and renewal after The Tower, while the Waite-Smith Empress wears twelve stars on the crown, often linked to the months or the zodiac. In reading practice a star rarely means arrival; it means orientation. The Olivia deck carves its stars in three ways: gold inlaid in the lapis night, ivory standing in relief, or plain lines cut into the stone. As you follow them, notice the material, where each star sits, and whether anyone looks up.
comparison: The Fool’s face is tipped straight towards a large gold star, high in the upper right. In the Two of Wands the star comes down to earth: small, ungilded, cut into the wall just below bare feet. The Empress does not wear the stars on the crown, as in the Waite-Smith card; twelve ivory stars ring the bowed head instead. The Chariot sets a gold star on the crown’s finial, directly above the forward-facing face. The King of Swords carries one at the blade’s tip, in place of the point. In the Five of Pentacles a gold star sits in the window’s tracery, high above both walkers. The Star ends with the great gold star above a bowed head.
prompt: Which light are you steering by at present, and do you still look up at it, or has it become part of the sky?

cards.name: The gold eight-pointed star
cards.seen: High in the upper right, a large eight-pointed star is inlaid in gold against the lapis night, far brighter than the scattered pyrite flecks around it. The Fool’s face is tipped straight towards it.
cards.meaning: Pamela Colman Smith gave the Fool a white sun; Olivia replaces it with a gold star, in a deck where gold is used sparingly. A star is a direction rather than a destination: something to steer by at night, when the ground ahead cannot yet be seen.

cards.name: The eight-pointed star
cards.seen: Carved into the face of the wall just below the figure’s bare feet, a small eight-pointed star in pale grey-blue lapis sits directly above the crossed flowers.
cards.meaning: The star is Olivia’s addition rather than part of the traditional card. Its eight points recall the gold star that leads Olivia’s Fool. Set in the wall itself, it suggests that a plan begins as an orienting light, long before it becomes a route.

cards.name: Twelve stars and a crown
cards.seen: Around the bowed head, twelve small five-pointed ivory stars stand in a ring against the lapis, framing a pointed ivory crown worn over long, wavy hair that falls past the shoulder.
cards.meaning: In the Waite-Smith card the twelve stars sit on the crown itself and are commonly read as the twelve months or the twelve signs of the zodiac: the whole turning year. Olivia lifts them off the crown into a halo, so the year surrounds the figure rather than being worn as a jewel.

cards.name: The gold star on the crown
cards.seen: A small eight-pointed gold star rises from a finial at the centre of the ivory crown. It stands against the lapis just beneath the starry arch, directly above the calm, forward-facing face.
cards.meaning: A star over the head is commonly read as the aim that steers the will: the charioteer is guided from above the crown, not by the crown itself. In a deck that uses gold sparingly, it crowns the card’s central axis, lined up above the gold disc on the car.

cards.name: Gold star at the tip
cards.seen: Where the blade would normally narrow to a point, it ends instead in a small round cap set with a gold eight-pointed star, the one gold accent on the ivory figure and its sword.
cards.meaning: A star replaces the blade’s point, so the sword leads with a fixed light rather than an edge. Stars in tarot suggest guidance and orientation, as in The Star. This is Olivia’s departure from the traditional image, and it reads as judgement steered by a principle, not by the wish to wound.

cards.name: The gold star above
cards.seen: At the crown of the window’s tracery, a solid five-pointed star inlaid in gold sits inside a carved roundel. Apart from small flecks in the night sky, it is the only gold on the card, set high above both figures.
cards.meaning: A star is traditionally a sign of orientation and hope, as in The Star. In the traditional image the whole window is bright stained glass; here the one bright point in the scene is this star, hanging above the walkers’ heads, unseen by either of them, and still there while they pass.

cards.name: The great gold star
cards.seen: At the centre of the sky hangs a large eight-pointed star in raised gold, four long rays alternating with four shorter ones, set in a soft haze of gold dust above the bowed head.
cards.meaning: An eight-pointed star in tarot often recalls Venus as morning and evening star, the light seen at dusk and before dawn. It is the only carved element on this card picked out in gold, so the eye keeps returning to it. The figure does not look up: the light works whether watched or not.

name: The sun
title: Daylight that keeps the night.
introduction: The sun is tarot’s plainest light. It has stood among the highest trumps since the fifteenth-century Italian decks, and medieval and Renaissance imagery used it for truth, clear sight and a warmth that reaches everyone alike. The Tarot de Marseille gives it a human face above two children and a low wall; the Golden Dawn assigned the card to the Sun itself, and the Waite-Smith image shows a single child on a white horse, with a banner and sunflowers. Readers commonly take it as clarity, vitality and joy that can be shared. Olivia gilds it in a deck that spends gold sparingly, yet some suns here are cool grey-blue lapis, and the sunflowers are lapis or ivory. Look, too, at what surrounds it: on every card of this trail, The Sun included, the sky is still a lapis night. The daylight does not erase the dark; it shines inside it. Follow where each sun sits and how much gold it receives.
comparison: On Death the sun is a gold half-disc resting on the far hills between two slim towers: light at a threshold. On Temperance it reaches a single summit, carved in grey-blue lapis, a quiet dawn rather than a blaze. In the Six of Swords a pale, open-eyed sun shares the sky with a thin crescent moon. The Lovers raises it overhead in gold, eyes closed above the angel. On The Sun it fills the upper sky, a large gold face with closed eyes, a band of stars running beside it. Finally the Queen of Wands holds one ivory sunflower whose face turns towards you: light taken in hand and offered on.
prompt: Where is there already enough light in your life to see clearly, and with whom could you share that warmth?

cards.name: The gold half-sun
cards.seen: On the far horizon, left of the banner staff, a gold half-disc rests on the line of the hills. Two slim lapis towers stand on the skyline, one near each side of the card.
cards.meaning: The sun on the horizon between two towers is a classic detail of this card, read as a threshold: light that is either leaving or arriving. It is the largest piece of gold on this card, set in the distance on the side the horse is walking towards.

cards.name: The sun on the peak
cards.seen: Above the tallest mountain a round disc of grey-blue lapis with a fine pale rim rests on the summit, its lower edge hidden by the rock, ringed with alternating long and short pointed rays.
cards.meaning: In the traditional image a path climbs from the pool towards a light between two peaks, commonly read as the goal of patient inner work. Olivia sets the light on a single summit and carves it in cool grey-blue lapis rather than gold: a quiet dawn at the end of a long road rather than a blaze.

cards.name: Sun-face and crescent together
cards.seen: At the upper right a pale grey-blue disc with a calm, open-eyed face sends out long, straight rays; at the upper left a thin crescent moon curves in lighter lapis. Gold flecks glitter in a diagonal band below them.
cards.meaning: The traditional Six of Swords has a plain sky. Olivia sets day and night in one sky, a between-time that suits a crossing. The rayed face also recalls the disc of The Moon: a hint that this passage is travelled partly by feel, not only by map.

cards.name: The gold sun, eyes closed
cards.seen: At the top centre, set clear above the angel’s head, a gold sun spreads straight, pointed rays against the lapis night. Its round face is calm, with the eyes closed.
cards.meaning: In the traditional image a great sun blazes directly behind the angel: full, conscious light over the whole scene. Olivia gilds it, in a deck where gold is used sparingly, but closes its eyes. The light is present without staring down; the choice below is left to the two who make it.

cards.name: The gilded sun face
cards.seen: A large gold disc fills the upper sky, carved with a calm, frontal face whose eyes are closed. Broad straight rays, thin spikes and wavy, flame-like rays alternate all the way around it.
cards.meaning: The sun with a human face appears on both Marseille and Waite-Smith cards as the source of warmth and plain sight. Here it is by far the largest area of gold on the card, and its closed eyes suggest a light that rests rather than stares.

cards.name: The sunflower in hand
cards.seen: In the Queen’s left hand, on the viewer’s right, a single ivory sunflower rises on a slender stalk with two broad leaves, its open face turned toward the viewer.
cards.meaning: The sunflower follows the sun and is commonly read as warmth, loyalty to what gives life, and joy that others can see. In the traditional card sunflowers appear in the Queen’s hand and on the throne; here one is held alone, a chosen, personal brightness rather than decoration.

name: The moon
title: From the crescent underfoot to the full disc.
introduction: Tarot’s moon comes from the old picture of the heavens, where the moon was the changeable light: linked with tides, moisture and growth, it waxed and waned while the sun stayed whole. The Marseille Moon shows a face above two towers, two dogs and a crayfish in a pool. The Golden Dawn gave the planet Moon to the High Priestess, and the Waite-Smith deck set a crescent at that figure’s feet, while its Moon card shows disc, crescent and face at once. In reading practice the moon points to cycles, dreams, instinct and what is not yet known. The Olivia deck carves it in ivory, pale lapis and gold. It is mostly a crescent, sometimes a full disc, and several times it appears on cards whose traditional image has no moon at all. As you follow it, notice its phase, its material and where it sits: behind, underfoot, worn or overhead.
comparison: In The Fool a pale crescent cradling a starry lapis disc lies on the rock behind the traveller, left rather than carried. The High Priestess rests the tip of a foot inside a large ivory crescent, horns upward: the cycle as ground to stand on. In The Chariot it is worn, a gold crescent on each shoulder plate. The Two of Swords hangs a gold crescent above a blindfolded choice; the King of Swords repeats it four times, along the throne and above the crown. Then the phase fills: the Eight of Cups shows a full lapis moon with closed eyes over a hooded traveller, and The Moon holds crescent and face together in one ivory disc ringed with rays.
prompt: What can you see only as a crescent so far, and what would it mean to let more of it show in its own time?

cards.name: The crescent and starry orb
cards.seen: On the rocky ground behind the Fool, at left, a pale silvery crescent cradles a disc of lapis set with small gold stars. Just above it, to the right, hangs an ivory sphere dotted with gold stars.
cards.meaning: Neither appears in the Waite-Smith Fool. The crescent belongs to the High Priestess and the Moon: cycles, the night mind, what is not yet known. The starry sphere reads as a small celestial globe. Both stay behind the traveller; the Fool carries neither.

cards.name: The crescent at the feet
cards.seen: At the hem of the pooled gown lies a large ivory crescent, horns turned upward, with the rounded tip of a foot resting inside its curve on the carved lapis floor.
cards.meaning: Kept from the Waite-Smith card, the crescent ties the High Priestess to the Moon, its Golden Dawn attribution, and is often compared with the figure in Revelation who has the moon underfoot. Resting on it, the figure is steadied by the cycle rather than ruled by it: tides, sleep, waxing and waning.

cards.name: Gold crescents on the shoulders
cards.seen: Each rounded shoulder plate of the ivory armour bears a gold crescent moon, both opening upward. Beneath them the breastplate is worked with fine carved ornament and a belt.
cards.meaning: Crescents on the shoulder plates belong to the traditional image and tie the card to the Moon and to Cancer, its sign in the Golden Dawn system. They suggest that this armour protects something tender and changeable rather than hiding it: strength shaped around feeling.

cards.name: The gold crescent moon
cards.seen: A slender crescent of gold hangs in the upper right, above the right-hand sword, its horns opening to the left. Small gold flecks scatter through the dark lapis sky around it.
cards.meaning: A crescent moon also appears in the traditional image, and it echoes the card’s Golden Dawn attribution, the Moon in Libra. The Moon is linked with feeling, instinct and tides, so a decision that looks purely mental is still moved by something quieter. It is the only large shape worked in gold here.

cards.name: Four gold crescents
cards.seen: Three pale gold crescent moons are set along the top block of the throne, the central one largest; a fourth crescent hangs inside the wreath directly above the crown.
cards.meaning: Crescent moons also belong to the traditional throne of this King. The moon stands for reflection, cycles and what is not yet fully seen; placed above the head of the suit’s most deliberate figure, it suggests that clear thinking still rests on intuition, rest and the slower tides of feeling.

cards.name: The moon with closed eyes
cards.seen: High on the right hangs a full, round moon carved in pale greyish blue lapis. Its face is turned slightly toward the left, eyes closed and lips shut, with small star shapes incised in the sky around it.
cards.meaning: The traditional image also gives this card a moon with a face, commonly read as an eclipse or a changing moon. Olivia shows a whole disc, asleep or inward. The traveller moves by night, without full daylight clarity, guided by feeling and quiet knowing rather than by proof.

cards.name: The crescent in the disc
cards.seen: A large ivory disc fills the upper centre, ringed by alternating straight and wavy rays. Carved in raised relief inside it, a crescent curves around the upper left, its lower horn ending at the brow of a face.
cards.meaning: The traditional Moon shows full disc, crescent and face at once, ringed by rays: a light that is borrowed and always changing phase. Olivia keeps all three in one ivory disc. The alternating straight and wavy rays can be read as two kinds of light mixed together here, steady fact and moving feeling.

name: The Milky Way
title: A road of stars carved in stone.
introduction: The Milky Way is not a traditional tarot symbol. Marseille cards and the Waite-Smith deck give you individual stars, a moon and a sun; no card in them gives the galaxy’s band a meaning of its own. Its lore lives elsewhere: the Greek tale of Hera’s spilled milk and the Greek word for milk, gala, that gives us galaxy; the medieval name Way of Saint James, linked with the pilgrims’ road to Santiago. This trail follows the Olivia deck’s own language. Every card rises from lapis lazuli, the stone medieval and Renaissance painters ground into ultramarine, and the stone brings its own sky: gold flecks of pyrite, pale mineral veins, hairline cracks. On many cards these gather into a glittering band that reads as the Milky Way. As you follow it, notice where it runs, above the figure or below, gold or silver, whole or broken, and how its place changes the mood of the scene.
comparison: Follow the band downwards. On The Magician it passes just beside the tip of the raised wand. On The Star it is a faint haze of white specks along a fine crack high in the sky. On The Hanged Man gold flecks slant down towards the bent knee and reappear below the halo. On the Page of Pentacles dense gold ends just beside the raised disc. On Judgement a narrow stream falls from beneath the clouds towards the mountains; on the Ace of Cups faceted crystals run down to the card’s edge. On the Ten of Cups it runs below the family, and on the Two of Swords it begins beneath the ledge that holds the seat.
prompt: Where does the wider sky sit in your life right now: overhead and out of reach, or already under your feet?

cards.name: The glittering Milky Way
cards.seen: A diagonal band of fine silvery sparkle runs from the top edge down to the left edge of the night sky, passing just beside the tip of the raised wand. It is far denser than the scattered gold star flecks.
cards.meaning: The traditional Magician stands against a plain yellow sky; Olivia sets the figure under the whole night instead. The wand is lifted into the same sky the galaxy crosses: a reminder that the Magician’s power comes from something larger and passes through one person.

cards.name: The Milky Way along the crack
cards.seen: A faint haze of white specks runs diagonally across the upper left sky, from near the top edge down toward the left pillar, following a fine crack in the lapis and dotted with gold flecks.
cards.meaning: The traditional Star has no Milky Way; this is Olivia’s addition. Because it follows a crack in the stone, light gathers along a break, which suits a card that comes straight after The Tower. Hope here is not the absence of damage; it grows along the line of it.

cards.name: The river of stars
cards.seen: A band of gold flecks enters at the top edge, slants down to the left towards the bent knee, and reappears below the halo, trailing away towards the lower right.
cards.meaning: The traditional image sets the figure against a plain ground; Olivia hangs it across the Milky Way. Upside down, the figure sees the stars inverted, yet the band still runs on behind the body: the larger order is still there, simply seen from a new angle.

cards.name: The river of gold flecks
cards.seen: Across the dark lapis sky, a diagonal band of dense gold flecks, with a few paler specks over a faint haze, runs from the upper right down towards the left, ending just left of the raised disc.
cards.meaning: The traditional Page stands under a plain daylit sky. Olivia sets the scene at night and threads a stream of gold through the stone, so the small gold star in the Page’s hands reads as one grain of a much larger field: the vast made studiable, one piece at a time.

cards.name: The falling trail of light
cards.seen: Left of the trumpet, a narrow diagonal stream of silver and gold chips runs from beneath the clouds down towards the mountain peaks on the left, denser and brighter than the scattered star flecks around it.
cards.meaning: This glittering band is Olivia’s addition, not part of the traditional card. It reads like a shooting star or a stretch of the Milky Way pouring towards the earth, echoing the trumpet: a line of light joining the sounding sky to the waiting ground.

cards.name: The glittering diagonal trail
cards.seen: Below the cloud’s left wing a trail of faceted, glittering crystals runs diagonally down to the left edge of the card, among small gold star flecks scattered across the dark lapis sky.
cards.meaning: This detail is Olivia’s own: what looks like a natural vein of crystals in the stone reads like a second overflow, light spilling from the sky as water spills from the cup. It hints that what the Ace offers can feel larger than one person, as wide as the night.

cards.name: The glittering mineral vein
cards.seen: From the left edge beside the figures, a pale band of glittering mineral runs diagonally down toward the lower centre of the dark lapis, among scattered gold star flecks and fine hairline cracks.
cards.meaning: This is natural stone rather than a carved symbol, but it is prominent here and reads like the Milky Way beneath the family’s feet. The night setting departs from the traditional daylight scene: contentment shown at the end of a day, lit from above.

cards.name: A glittering vein below
cards.seen: From just beneath the ledge a diagonal vein of pale, sparkling mineral runs down toward the lower left across the dark lapis, catching light in tiny blue and white points.
cards.meaning: This is the stone’s own marking rather than a traditional symbol. In a card about withheld sight, it adds a trail of light leading down and away from the seat, a quiet hint that there is a path out of the stillness once the figure is ready to take it.

name: Flame
title: A small fire, carried by hand.
introduction: Fire came into tarot slowly. In Marseille-pattern decks the suit of Batons is drawn as wooden staves and clubs, though the Hermit already raises a lantern. The Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn tied Wands firmly to Fire in the late nineteenth century, and the Waite-Smith deck of 1909 made the link visible: staves that sprout leaves, salamanders patterned on the Wands court, the creature that medieval bestiaries and later Paracelsus placed at home in flame. In readings, fire tends to stand for will, desire and the spark that makes you begin; what matters is what the flame is doing and who holds it. Olivia keeps its fire small and precious. On lapis and ivory it is most often a point of gold: at the tip of a staff, on the branches of a tree, inside a lantern. As you follow it, notice where the gold sits and which way the flame turns.
comparison: The Ace of Wands shows a closed gold bud in ivory sepals; the Page of Wands raises a matching shape, half bud and half flame, above a tunic of salamanders. In The Lovers the flames multiply: eighteen gold flames on a blue tree. On the Seven of Wands a crown of flame rises beyond the fist; the Knight of Wands holds it forward, tongues bent back as if by a headwind. The King of Wands sets polished gold above an ivory cup of petals on a flowering staff. The Devil grips an ivory torch slanting down, its flame still curling upward, and in The Hermit the light is enclosed: a gold star in a lantern held out at chest height.
prompt: Which fire are you carrying now: a closed bud, a flame held forward, a torch turned down, or a lantern for the next step?

cards.name: The gold flame-bud
cards.seen: At the top of the staff sits a closed bud of gold, its pointed petals rising together like a single flame, cupped in ivory sepals. It is the only gilded part of the carving.
cards.meaning: Wands belong to Fire, and the traditional Ace is often surrounded by sparks or flame-like leaves. Olivia gathers that fire into one golden bud that has not yet opened: energy concentrated at the very tip, still held in, ready to become flower or flame.

cards.name: The gold flame-bud
cards.seen: At the tip of the staff, two upward-curving ivory sepals cup a pointed shape of gold, half bud and half flame; it is the brightest point on the card.
cards.meaning: In the traditional image the Page’s wand sprouts green leaves, a sign of living growth. Here the staff is bare and ends in a closed gold bud that is also a flame, the same bud that crowns Olivia’s Ace of Wands: the spark is real and precious, but has not yet opened.

cards.name: The tree of gold flames
cards.seen: Behind the right-hand figure a slender blue tree carries eighteen small gold flames among its carved leaves. Apart from the sun and the scattered gold flecks in the sky, they are the only gold on the card.
cards.meaning: Waite called this the Tree of Life bearing twelve fruits, and its flames are commonly read as the twelve signs of the zodiac: passion and spirit. Olivia’s tree carries more than the traditional twelve and gilds every one, so desire here is warm and plentiful, not rationed.

cards.name: Gold flame on the staff
cards.seen: At the staff’s left-hand end, just beyond the left fist, a small crown of gold flame curls upward in several tongues. It is the only gold on the figure or the rock.
cards.meaning: Wands are the suit of Fire: will, conviction and creative drive. Traditional Wands are living wood, often sprouting leaves; this staff ends in a flame instead. What is being defended is not only ground but a fire of your own, kept close to the hand and behind the guard.

cards.name: The gold flame
cards.seen: At the far end of the wand a gold flame rises in several curling tongues, bending slightly back as if in a headwind; with the scattered star flecks, it is the only gold on the card.
cards.meaning: Wands belong to fire, and as Fire of Fire this Knight is the suit’s element in its most concentrated court form. In the traditional image the rod sprouts green leaves; here it burns instead. The living growth has become open flame: energy at its most visible, and also at its least contained.

cards.name: The gold flame
cards.seen: At the top of the staff, above a small ivory cup of petals, a flame of polished gold rises in several tongues; it is the only gold on the figure and the throne.
cards.meaning: Wands are the suit of fire: will, creative drive, the spark that makes you begin. The traditional King holds a sprouting branch; Olivia sets living fire on its tip and turns the branch into a torch. Vision here is not kept private; it is a light others can see by.

cards.name: The torch held low
cards.seen: The Devil’s left hand grips an ivory torch that slants down and outward to the viewer’s right, past the corner of the block. The flame burns at the lower end and curls upward in long tongues.
cards.meaning: The traditional Devil holds a torch turned toward the earth, commonly read as fire spent downward: desire and energy poured into matter instead of lighting the way. The flame still rises, which is the hopeful detail. The same heat that feeds a habit can be turned to something you choose.

cards.name: The lantern with its gold star
cards.seen: Held out at about chest height, an ivory lantern with a peaked roof and panelled sides hangs from a ring in the fingers. Inside is a small gold eight-pointed star, the only carved element picked out in gold.
cards.meaning: In the Waite-Smith card the lantern holds a six-pointed star, and older models often show it half-wrapped in the cloak. Olivia gives the star eight points, matching the two stars cut into the rock, and holds the lantern fully out: a light for the next few steps, not for the whole mountain.

name: Weather
title: Clouds that give, storms that clear.
introduction: Weather has long been one of tarot’s ways of picturing what cannot be held. Renaissance emblem books often show a hand reaching out of the clouds, a sign of help or action from beyond human reach, and Marseille decks already give the Aces of Batons and Swords a hand from a cloud. In the Waite-Smith deck of 1909 all four Aces receive their gift from a cloud, lightning strikes the Tower, rain falls on the Three of Swords and a rainbow arches over the Ten of Cups. In the Golden Dawn system Swords belong to Air, so clouds on Swords cards are commonly read as the weather of the mind: moods, worries and thoughts that gather and pass. Olivia carves the clouds that give in ivory and the storm clouds in paler lapis, and sets the bolt in inlaid gold. As you follow the trail, notice whether the weather is giving, hiding, breaking or clearing.
comparison: On the Ace of Wands an ivory cloud carved in tight spirals billows highest where the hand emerges; on the Ace of Pentacles a dense ivory bank releases the wrist. On The Moon two soft ivory clouds drift beside the disc and cover part of its rays. On the Seven of Wands lapis clouds curl and stream sideways behind the figure, among fine wind lines. The Tower’s gold bolt, symbolic change rather than a forecast, leaves the cloud and strikes the crown. On the Three of Swords rain slants around the blade points; on the Ten of Swords the clouds sit low beneath an open, starry night. The Ten of Cups closes with the rainbow carved as a stone arch.
prompt: What weather is moving through your mind today, and what might it be carrying, hiding or clearing away?

cards.name: Spiralling ivory cloud
cards.seen: A broad ivory cloud crosses the card from the left edge to the right, its surface carved into tight spirals and scrolls; it billows highest on the right, where the hand emerges.
cards.meaning: The cloud marks the source as unseen: the spark comes from beyond what you can plan or explain. Its whirling spirals, carved like wind or smoke, bring a sense of stirring energy into an otherwise still and upright image.

cards.name: The cloud at the edge
cards.seen: A dense bank of ivory cloud, carved in soft rounded masses with lapis showing through its gaps, fills the right edge; the wrist emerges from it and wisps trail left beneath the hand.
cards.meaning: The cloud is the traditional source of the Aces, a reminder that openings often arrive from beyond your planning. Here it also runs underneath the hand like a support, so what comes from outside is steadied as it is offered.

cards.name: The clouds across the disc
cards.seen: Two soft ivory clouds drift at either side of the disc. The left one crosses the lower edge of the disc and its rays; the right one lies over the rays at the lower right.
cards.meaning: Clouds are Olivia’s addition; the traditional Moon hangs in a clear sky. They build partial cover into the image itself: some of the light is hidden, and nothing is wrong because of it. The card works with half-seen things, and the clouds make that literal.

cards.name: Wind-driven clouds
cards.seen: Behind the head and shoulders, clouds carved in lighter blue lapis curl and stream sideways, and fine wind lines run horizontally behind the figure’s arms and torso on both sides.
cards.meaning: In the Wands suit, air feeds fire as much as it tests it. These clouds add a headwind of opinion, noise and strain. The figure does not rise above the weather but stands inside it and keeps position anyway.

cards.name: The gold lightning bolt
cards.seen: A bolt of inlaid gold leaves the underside of the cloud, zigzags down to the right and strikes the crown at the tower’s summit, where a thread of gold runs on into a crack in its band.
cards.meaning: Lightning is the classic image of a sudden insight or a truth that arrives from outside a closed system. It is the brightest gold on this card and it touches only the crown, so the strike is aimed at what sits on top: a claim, a certainty, a pretence of control.

cards.name: Slanting incised rain
cards.seen: Fine pale lines are scratched into the lapis below the cloud line, slanting from upper right to lower left and filling both sides of the lower card around the blade points.
cards.meaning: Rain is the classic weather of this card, often read as tears and as release. Rain also washes and waters. Its steady slant gives the image movement: grief falling through, not frozen in place, which is where the card’s quiet hope begins.

cards.name: Low bank of clouds
cards.seen: Heavy, billowing clouds carved in lighter greyish blue lapis fill the middle band of the card behind the sword hilts, rising highest on the left and thinning toward the horizon on the right.
cards.meaning: Clouds in the Swords suit usually mark a troubled or overworked mind. Here they sit low, between the sea and the open sky, as if the storm has already passed over and settled behind the scene. Above them the night is clear.

cards.name: The carved stone arch
cards.seen: A broad band of paler, greyer lapis rises from the left near the figures’ raised hands, curves in a near semicircle above the cottage and comes down on the right, framing the valley like a window.
cards.meaning: In the traditional card this is a rainbow in full colour, a classic image of peace after a storm. Olivia carves it in plain stone, turning passing light into something built: harmony here is a structure people make and keep up, not weather that simply arrives.

name: Water
title: From the measured pour to the night pool.
introduction: Water is one of tarot’s oldest images. The figure of Temperance already pours between two vessels in fifteenth-century Italian decks; the Marseille Star kneels to empty two jugs onto the water, and a crayfish lies in the pool beneath The Moon. In the Golden Dawn system Cups belong to the element of Water, and once Pamela Colman Smith gave the numbered cards scenes in 1909, water spread across the whole deck: rivers, seas and pools that readers commonly take as feeling, intuition and the unconscious. In the Olivia deck water is carved, not painted. Poured water falls in smooth, pale, deliberate threads; rivers and seas are cut into the lapis in lighter blues, scored with ripples, while pools lie dark; gold touches it rarely, as a thin line along a far shore or the foot of a golden path. As you follow it, notice where water is held, where it moves freely and where it hides something below.
comparison: In Temperance an ivory stream arcs from a raised goblet into a lower one: water measured and mixed. In The Star a raised jug returns a single thread to the pool. The Ace of Cups overflows, five glassy streams falling and rippling where they land. In the Eight of Cups a river runs past the cups instead of filling them, and in the Knight of Cups a row of stones lies across a stream. In the Six of Swords flat water leads to a far shore traced with gold. Around the King of Cups the sea curls into spirals against the dais, and in The Moon a crayfish rests in the dark pool where the gold path begins.
prompt: Which water is closest to your life right now: the measured pour, the moving river, the wide sea or the pool at night?

cards.name: The stream between two goblets
cards.seen: The figure holds a stemmed ivory goblet high on the viewer’s left and tilts it; a smooth ivory stream arcs down into a second goblet held lower, near the waist, in the other hand.
cards.meaning: Pouring between two vessels is the card’s oldest feature, commonly linked with the ancient habit of tempering wine with water. It is not about emptying one cup to fill another but about mixing in a continuous, deliberate flow. The lowered eyes follow the stream closely, as though the measure matters.

cards.name: The jug raised high
cards.seen: At the left, one ivory arm lifts a jug above shoulder height, the hand gripping its handle, and tips it so a single clear thread of water falls straight down into the pool, raising rings.
cards.meaning: In the traditional reading the water poured into the pool returns to its source: feeling and attention given back to the deep reserve they came from. The jug is lifted high and held steady. Refilling the source is shown as deliberate care, not an accident of overflow.

cards.name: Five streams to the pool
cards.seen: Four glassy streams rise from inside the bowl and arch over the rim, two to each side; a fifth drops straight down the centre below the foot. All five reach the pool, with drops falling between them.
cards.meaning: The overflowing fountain is the heart of this card: more than the cup can hold, given freely. The five streams of the traditional image are commonly read as the five senses. Here the water falls in clean, steady lines and ripples where it lands, abundant but not flooding.

cards.name: The winding river
cards.seen: A river winds out of the hills on the left, runs behind the cups and breaks into white water over rocks at the lower right, between the cups and the traveller’s path.
cards.meaning: Water appears at the foot of the traditional image as well. Cups are Water, and here that water keeps moving past the cups rather than filling them. Feeling does not stay where it was poured; the river quietly separates what is kept from what is sought.

cards.name: Stream and a row of stones
cards.seen: A stream winds from the far hills across the left of the scene towards the horse’s raised hoof, with a row of rounded stones lying across it just ahead; trees stand on the banks beyond.
cards.meaning: Water is the suit’s element, and in the traditional card the Knight approaches a river. Olivia adds a row of stones like stepping stones: a way across that asks for attention at every step. Deep feeling can be crossed, the image suggests, not with a leap but stone by stone.

cards.name: The gilded far shore
cards.seen: Beyond the boat the water lies flat and finely lined. Across it, a low bank of rounded lapis trees runs the width of the card, and a thin vein of gold traces the waterline along most of its length.
cards.meaning: In the traditional image the further shore is simply where the passage leads. Olivia marks it with the card’s one sustained line of gold, quietly and without drama. Calmer ground exists and is already visible across the water, even while the crossing is still under way in the chop.

cards.name: The rolling waves
cards.seen: A broad band of sea in deep and pale blue lapis crosses the lower card, its crests curling into small spirals that break against the dais, above a plain dark lapis margin.
cards.meaning: Water is the suit’s element, and a restless sea around the throne is traditional for this King. The waves are active, even turbulent, while the figure sits still: the card concerns not the absence of strong feeling but a calm response in its presence.

cards.name: The crayfish in the pool
cards.seen: At the bottom centre, a crayfish carved in grey-blue lapis rests in the dark pool, both claws raised, its long feelers curving up along the gold where the path begins.
cards.meaning: The creature in the pool is one of the oldest features of the card, commonly read as something from the deep mind rising toward awareness: an early, half-formed feeling or memory. Olivia sets it at the very foot of the gold path, so the way through the night begins with what surfaces.

name: Mountains
title: From the cliff edge to the horizon.
introduction: Mountains are rare in early tarot. Marseille-pattern cards mostly set their figures on a bare strip of ground, and the peaks most readers know were drawn by Pamela Colman Smith for the Waite-Smith deck of 1909: the Fool at a precipice, the Hermit on a snowy height, the Emperor before bare ranges. The image has an older echo. Since Hesiod, writers have placed Virtue at the top of a steep, hard road, and some Renaissance pictures of Hercules at the crossroads show that road climbing a rocky hill. In reading practice, mountains stand for aims still far off, hard facts that do not move, and ground firm enough to stand on. The Olivia deck carves its mountains in the lapis itself, in paler, greyer blues rather than ivory or gold: they are cut from the same stone as the night sky. As you follow them, watch the distance. Is the rock underfoot, behind the figure, or out on the horizon?
comparison: The Fool strides across a veined outcrop that breaks off in a sheer face, the leading foot just short of the rim. On the Ten of Swords the figure lies on a broad, chipped ledge of bright blue lapis: rough, but solid. The Hermit stands on a pale shelf above a drop, with two snow-streaked peaks rising behind. Behind The Emperor, jagged peaks rise on both sides of the throne with nothing growing on them. In the Ace of Swords, the blade points down into the gap between two steep peaks. On the Page of Pentacles one broad peak sits far behind the figure, at waist height. On Judgement, a pale range stretches across the whole horizon beyond the sea.
prompt: Which mountain in your life right now is ground to stand on, and which is a peak you are only looking at?

cards.name: The lapis cliff edge
cards.seen: The Fool strides barefoot across a flat-topped outcrop of lighter, veined lapis that breaks off in a sheer carved face to the right, the leading foot planted just short of the rim. Blue peaks rise far behind on the left.
cards.meaning: The precipice is the card’s defining risk: the moment the familiar ground runs out. Here the leading foot still rests on stone and the next stride is not yet taken, which leaves a moment for choice: a leap or a pause.

cards.name: The lapis rock ledge
cards.seen: The figure lies on a broad, flat ledge of rough, bright blue lapis, its surface chipped and textured with lighter veins, dropping away to darker, cracked stone along the bottom of the card.
cards.meaning: The ledge is the Ten’s literal bottom: there is nowhere lower to fall. In the Golden Dawn scheme the tens belong to Malkuth, the Kingdom, the most solid level of the Tree of Life, and this stone makes that concrete. A floor is also something to stand up from.

cards.name: The pale mountain range
cards.seen: Behind the figure, two main peaks and their ridges are carved in lighter, greyer lapis, streaked like snow and wind-scoured stone, above a long sloping shelf that breaks off sharply at the left.
cards.meaning: Mountains in tarot stand for effort, altitude and the long view, and the Waite-Smith Hermit stands on a snowy height. Olivia keeps the cold, high setting but lets the peaks rise behind the figure: the top is not reached, and the work here is looking rather than climbing.

cards.name: The bare lapis peaks
cards.seen: Jagged mountains carved in paler grey-blue lapis rise behind the throne on both sides, their ridges sharply faceted; the tallest peak rises above the throne back, just to the right of the crown. Nothing grows on them, and no water runs below.
cards.meaning: The Waite-Smith Emperor also sits before bare mountains, commonly read as hard-won stability and the discipline of high, dry ground. A thin stream at their foot is traditional; Olivia leaves it out, so the scene holds only stone: firm footing, with little to soften it.

cards.name: Twin peaks in lapis
cards.seen: Two steep, faceted peaks rise in the lower third in lighter blue lapis, with smaller ridges at either edge and a level horizon behind; the sword’s tip points into the gap between them.
cards.meaning: Mountains also sit below the sword in Pamela Colman Smith’s version of this Ace, commonly read as hard facts, difficulty and the heights thought can reach. Here the blade points into the gap between two peaks: the passage through a problem rather than a view over it.

cards.name: A single distant peak
cards.seen: On the right, low hills rise to one broad peak carved in greyer lapis, with a thin band of cloud above it; it sits far behind the figure, at the level of the waist.
cards.meaning: A distant mountain is part of the traditional scene, and in tarot mountains often stand for an aim that takes effort to reach. Here it is small and far off, behind the Page, while the gaze stays on the disc: mastery exists, but today’s work is closer.

cards.name: The pale mountain range
cards.seen: Beyond the sea, a range of pale grey-blue peaks carved in the lapis stretches across the whole horizon, rising highest near each side of the card and dipping low behind the banner.
cards.meaning: Mountains in tarot are commonly read as height, abstract thought and the long view. On Judgement they belong to the traditional scene as the horizon that waking reveals: once the call is heard, the view reaches much further than it did from inside the coffin.

name: The way
title: Roads that bend, boats that carry you across.
introduction: Roads, boats and bridges are tarot’s grammar of passage. Older European imagery already used them this way: the pilgrim’s road, Hercules choosing between two ways, the storm-tossed ship of the Renaissance emblem books. In the Marseille pattern the numbered Minor cards are ornamental arrangements without landscape, so most of the roads, ships and bridges you meet in the suits arrive with Pamela Colman Smith’s scenes for A. E. Waite’s 1909 deck, where they became a reader’s shorthand for transition: leaving, crossing, carrying on. In the Olivia deck these routes are mostly carved into the lapis itself, in pale or greyish blue, so they read as part of the landscape rather than as ornament. Two exceptions stand out on this trail: the boat of the Six of Swords is ivory, and the road of The Moon is gold. As you follow it, notice where each way starts, whether you can see its end, and who is on it.
comparison: On the Ace of Pentacles a path winds from the hedge arch towards the mountains: the way is only offered. In the Three of Wands three ships are already under sail. In the Five of Cups a small arched bridge stands behind the bowed figure, its far end hidden by the cloak. The Six of Swords is the crossing, an ivory boat in choppy water. In the Ten of Wands a pale road winds between fields to the town gate. Death sets a lone rower on a winding river. Temperance’s path winds up from the pool and disappears behind the figure; The Moon’s gold road climbs from the water into a gap in the mountains, its end out of sight.
prompt: Which crossing are you in the middle of now, and what is holding you up while the water is still rough?

cards.name: The path to the mountains
cards.seen: Carved in pale lapis, a narrow path winds from the hedge arch back through low hills toward a range of mountains with one peak higher than the rest.
cards.meaning: Traditionally the path beyond the garden leads to the mountains of long effort and larger aims. It shows that this Ace is a beginning with somewhere to go; the gift in the hand becomes meaningful only when you walk it out into the world.

cards.name: Three ships under sail
cards.seen: On the sea below, three small ships carved in pale lapis sail with canvas set: one further out, between the left wand and the figure, and two nearer the viewer, close to the left and right edges.
cards.meaning: Ships are the card’s traditional picture of ventures sent out: trade, messages, plans travelling toward distant shores. Seen from above, they are already under way. They invite patience with a process that no longer needs you at the helm, and attention to what may come back.

cards.name: The arched bridge
cards.seen: Behind the figure a small stone bridge with a single rounded arch crosses the river, carved in muted blue lapis. Its far end disappears behind the ivory cloak.
cards.meaning: A bridge appears in the traditional image too, often read as the way across from grief toward what comes next. Here it lies at the figure’s back, partly hidden by the cloak: a crossing that exists, but that the moment of loss does not need to hurry toward.

cards.name: The ivory boat in choppy water
cards.seen: A plain, long, shallow ivory boat with a raised prow at the left and a small crossbar near the stern. Pale-crested waves ripple around its hull; with the pole pushing back to the right, it travels left.
cards.meaning: A boat is tarot’s image of passage: crossing from one state to another with something to hold you up. Smith’s card is often read as moving from rough water towards smoother water. Here the chop surrounds the boat itself: the crossing happens inside the unsettled part, not after it.

cards.name: The winding road
cards.seen: A pale road winds up from the flat ground ahead of the figure’s front foot, curving between furrowed fields and trees until it reaches the arched gate of the town.
cards.meaning: The road is not straight: it winds in curves on its way to the gate. It adds a detail the traditional image leaves implicit, that the last stretch of a long effort often feels longer than it looks, and that the way still leads somewhere.

cards.name: The river and boat
cards.seen: A river winds from the horizon down the left side of the card in pale, rippled lapis. Near the lower bend a small boat carries one seated figure holding an oar.
cards.meaning: The river and boat of the traditional image are often compared with the crossing to the far shore in older myths. Water keeps moving without losing itself, and the lone rower suggests that every passage through change is made one stroke at a time.

cards.name: The winding path
cards.seen: From the stony bank at the right of the pool a pale, finely textured path winds up the slope and disappears behind the figure. A thinner winding line crosses the slopes on the left, beside the irises.
cards.meaning: The path from the water to the heights is a classic feature of Temperance, commonly read as the long road of gradual integration. It bends back and forth rather than climbing straight, a reminder that balance is reached adjustment by adjustment, not in one decisive leap.

cards.name: The gold path
cards.seen: A winding road of gold leaf starts in the pool, its gold spilling across the water, climbs between the two animals and the castles, narrows, and disappears into a gap in the mountains.
cards.meaning: The path between the towers is constant in the traditional Moon, commonly read as the way through uncertainty toward what cannot yet be seen. Olivia gilds it, the only carved element laid in gold, while the moon itself stays ivory. The route is clear even where its end is not.

name: Rose and lily
title: From the tended garden to the white rose.
introduction: In medieval and Renaissance images of the Virgin, painters often paired the rose and the lily: the lily of the Annunciation for purity, the rose for love. When Pamela Colman Smith painted Waite’s deck in 1909, she set roses and lilies around the Magician’s table, and Waite read them as flowers of the field changed into garden flowers: cultivated aspiration. Readers commonly take the rose as desire and love, the lily as purity of intention, and the pair as wanting something with a clean motive. Smith returned to the rose elsewhere, most memorably the white rose in the Fool’s hand and on Death’s banner. The Olivia deck carves these flowers in three materials: lapis roses and lilies in gardens and on robes, ivory roses held, worn or raised, and one rose inlaid in gold. As you follow them, notice the pair giving way to a single rose, and whether each flower is planted, worn, held or let go.
comparison: In the Ace of Pentacles lilies grow on the left of the garden, roses on the right. In the Two of Wands a lapis rose and a paler lily cross their stems into an X. The Hierophant’s two kneelers carry the pair on their backs: roses on one robe, a lily on the other. Then the rose goes on alone. An arbour of roses arches over the throne of the Queen of Pentacles; in Strength an ivory chain of them slips off the gown. In the Nine of Swords one rose inlaid in gold lies below the hanging hand. The Fool carries a single ivory rose held low, and Death raises one, carved on a pale banner.
prompt: Where in your life are desire and clear intention growing side by side, and where has one crowded out the other?

cards.name: The lilies on the left
cards.seen: Tall lilies with open, star-shaped blooms and long pointed leaves stand in a cluster on the left, carved in lighter blue lapis and rising above the top of the hedge.
cards.meaning: Lilies grow in the traditional Ace of Pentacles garden and are commonly read as purity of intention. They suggest that what grows here grows best from a clean motive: tending a thing for its own sake, not only for what it could return.

cards.name: The crossed rose and lily
cards.seen: Below the star, a full-blown rose in grey-blue lapis and an open lily in a paler, almost ivory tone are carved in relief, their leafy stems crossing in an X, with tufts of grass on either side.
cards.meaning: Waite asked readers to notice a rose, cross and lily on this card. The pairing recalls the Magician’s garden, commonly read as desire joined to pure intention. Here the crossed stems themselves make the cross, set at the centre of the wall’s foot: the plan above rests on both.

cards.name: The kneeler with roses
cards.seen: At the lower left a figure kneels with back turned, carved in pale blue lapis. Two roses with leaves are incised in fine light lines across the robe’s back; the soles of both feet show beneath the hem.
cards.meaning: In the traditional image the two ministers wear roses and lilies, the flowers of the Magician’s garden. The rose is commonly read as desire and love. Here the student carries it on the back: the longing that brings someone to a teaching, seen more clearly by others than by oneself.

cards.name: The rose arbour
cards.seen: A lapis rose vine climbs from both sides of the throne and meets in an arch above it, carved with open roses, tight buds and serrated leaves in paler blue relief against the starred night.
cards.meaning: Roses in the suit of Pentacles speak of cultivated beauty: something grown, pruned and tended over seasons rather than bought. The arbour frames the Queen as the keeper of a garden, so the care this card describes reads as ongoing work, not a single gift.

cards.name: The chain of roses
cards.seen: From the figure’s waist, a chain of small carved ivory roses and buds crosses the gown diagonally towards the hip and thigh, then slips off the drapery and trails loose to the right, ending in a bud.
cards.meaning: Roses are commonly read as desire and love that have been cultivated. In the traditional image a flower garland also links the figure to the lion, a gentle bond many readers dwell on. Here the garland hangs only from the gown: the bond between them is carried by the hands alone.

cards.name: The single gold rose
cards.seen: On the quilt, a little below the hanging hand, one rose is inlaid in gold with a short stem and two leaves. It is the only gold anywhere on the bed or bedclothes.
cards.meaning: Roses in tarot speak of beauty, love and what still blooms. The traditional quilt carries many roses; Olivia gilds just one. Close to the resting hand, it quietly marks something precious and intact that the covered eyes are not yet seeing.

cards.name: The white rose
cards.seen: In the trailing hand, held low beside the wind-pulled robe, the Fool carries a single open ivory rose on a short stem with a few small leaves.
cards.meaning: Smith’s Fool also holds a white rose, commonly read as innocence and a desire free of grasping. One flower, not a bouquet: a single uncomplicated wish, held loosely enough that it does not slow the pace.

cards.name: The rose on the banner
cards.seen: A long ivory banner hangs from a crossbar on a staff whose tip rises above it like a cross. In its lower half a single full-blown rose is carved in relief, with four leaves on its stem.
cards.meaning: Death’s banner traditionally carries a white rose, commonly read as purity and life that continues through change. Smith set it on a black flag; here banner and rose are the same pale ivory, so the flag reads less as mourning and more as a standard of quiet renewal.

name: Harvest
title: Everything ripe was once waited for.
introduction: Growing things have long served European art as images of time. The medieval Labours of the Months set reaping in summer and the grape harvest in autumn; Christian imagery read wheat and the vine as bread and wine, and wheat belonged to Ceres, Roman goddess of the harvest. The Tarot de Marseille decorates its numbered coins with stylised foliage rather than scenes, and hangs the Hanged Man between two lopped trees. The Golden Dawn titled the Seven of Pentacles “Success Unfulfilled”; the Waite-Smith deck planted whole gardens: a figure leaning on a hoe before a bush of discs, a lone figure in a vineyard, a King robed in grapes, the Empress behind ripe wheat. Readers commonly take these plants as growth that cannot be hurried. Here Olivia carves every plant in lapis, paler or greyer than the night, and saves its gold for other things. Follow the growth from cut wood to a harvest someone stands on.
comparison: On The Hanged Man two living trees stand with their side branches sawn back to stubs: growth begins with something cut away. In the Seven of Pentacles a paler lapis bush has risen from worked soil above the figure’s head, while the figure leans on the spade, gaze turned upward. The Empress lets tall ripe wheat fill the whole lower third, heavy ears bending every way. In the Three of Cups grapes sit in beaded clusters in the garland beneath the dancers’ feet. The Nine of Pentacles rests one bare hand lightly above a heavy cluster, not picking it. Finally the King of Pentacles sets a sandalled foot on a vine covering the ground beneath the throne.
prompt: What in your life is still ripening at its own pace, and what small tending could you offer it today?

cards.name: Two pruned living trees
cards.seen: Two lapis trunks rise on either side of the figure, their side branches sawn back to round stubs. At the top each trunk forks into a Y that holds the beam, one arm ending in a ringed, cut stump.
cards.meaning: Marseille decks hang the figure between two trees with lopped branches; the Waite-Smith card uses a single T-shaped tree in leaf. Olivia returns to the pair. Cut back yet still alive, the trees suggest pruning: something taken away so that growth can go elsewhere.

cards.name: The tall pale-blue bush
cards.seen: A branching bush carved in lighter lapis rises from the soil at the right to above the figure’s head, its stems covered in deeply cut, serrated leaves; a smaller sprig grows behind the figure’s back.
cards.meaning: The plant is the long investment itself: something that grew slowly from ground that was worked. Traditionally it is green; here it is carved from the same blue stone as the night, only paler, a living thing half merged with its background, as growth often is when you are standing close to it.

cards.name: The field of wheat
cards.seen: The whole lower third is filled with tall, ripe wheat carved in blue-grey relief, heavy ears bending in different directions, rising around the couch leg and the edge of the paving.
cards.meaning: Ripe grain grows before the Waite-Smith Empress as well, and wheat is the plant of Demeter and Ceres, goddesses of the harvest. It shows abundance as something grown over a season, not conjured: tended, waited for, then gathered. Here the field reaches right to the viewer’s edge.

cards.name: Clusters of grapes
cards.seen: Several bunches of grapes, carved as tight beaded clusters in blue-grey lapis, sit among the gourds and vine leaves of the garland, the largest at its lower right, below the right-hand dancer’s feet.
cards.meaning: Grapes are an ancient sign of festivity and of wine shared at table. In a suit of Water they recall that feeling ferments and deepens with time, and gently hint that celebration is richest when it is not drunk too fast.

cards.name: The bare hand on the grapes
cards.seen: The other hand hangs ungloved at right, fingertips resting lightly on the vine stem just above a heavy cluster of grapes. The veiled head is bowed, eyes lowered, looking at neither bird nor fruit.
cards.meaning: Grapes are the classic Pentacles sign of harvest and slow-ripened pleasure: wine takes seasons. One hand is gloved for discipline, the other bare for enjoyment. The touch is light; the figure is not picking or counting, only appreciating what has grown.

cards.name: The vine underfoot
cards.seen: A lapis grapevine spreads across the raised ground beneath the throne, heavy with grape clusters and broad lobed leaves; tendrils climb both sides of the seat, and one sandalled ivory foot rests on the vine-covered ground.
cards.meaning: Grapes stand for harvest that takes years: vines are planted long before they bear fruit. Spread under the King’s foot, they show a life standing on cultivated plenty. The same vine runs through robe, throne and ground, so figure, seat and earth share one harvest.

name: Thresholds
title: What stands between, and the crossing.
introduction: Tarot is full of doorways. Its paired columns go back to Jachin and Boaz, the two bronze pillars before Solomon’s Temple in the Book of Kings, which the Golden Dawn raised in its ritual hall; the Waite-Smith deck of 1909 letters them B and J beside the High Priestess. The Marseille Papesse already sits before a curtain, and in reading practice the veil is commonly taken as knowledge held back until you are ready for it. Walls, arches and windows draw on older images too: the enclosed garden of medieval devotion, or the Waite-Smith Five of Pentacles, two figures in snow beneath a stained-glass window. A threshold rarely asks which side is right; it asks where you are standing. Olivia carves these boundaries in lapis, cut from the same stone as the night around them, with the ivory figures set in front. Notice whether each one holds you, hides something or lets you through.
comparison: The High Priestess sits between two pillars, and the dark, unlettered one is only half of the pair. The Hierophant has pillars at either side, no throne back carved between them. Justice sits before a plain greyish veil slung between the pillar tops; the Nine of Cups hangs a pale, tasselled curtain beneath its shelf of cups. On the Five of Pentacles a shawled figure walks past an unlit Gothic window, snow on its sill. On The Star the figure kneels between two slender columns framing the pool and star. The Ace of Pentacles opens a rose-wreathed arch in the hedge for the path, and on The Sun the lapis wall finally stands at the child’s back.
prompt: Where are you standing right now: between two pillars, behind a curtain, or already stepping through the arch?

cards.name: The dark pillar
cards.seen: On the viewer’s left stands a column of deep ultramarine lapis with a rough, pitted shaft, a leafy capital with curled corner volutes and a stepped base. No letter is carved on it.
cards.meaning: In the Waite-Smith card this is Boaz, marked B, one of the two bronze pillars before Solomon’s Temple. It is commonly read as the receptive, unseen side of any polarity: night, rest, what has not yet been spoken. Olivia leaves it unlettered, so texture alone carries the contrast.

cards.name: Two lapis pillars
cards.seen: Two blue columns stand at either side, carved in the lapis itself, with scrolled capitals and stepped bases. The left shaft catches more light than the right. No throne back is carved between them.
cards.meaning: Pillars mark the threshold of a temple, and the traditional Hierophant sits between a grey pair that echoes the High Priestess’s. Here they stand well apart from the figure, framing an open space: the doorway of an institution, a place where knowledge is kept and entered.

cards.name: The swagged lapis veil
cards.seen: A plain cloth carved in lighter, greyish lapis is slung between the tops of the two pillars, sagging in a shallow curve and falling in soft vertical folds behind the figure’s crown and shoulders.
cards.meaning: A veil hangs behind the seated figure in the traditional card too, echoing the High Priestess. Unlike the Priestess’s veil, this one carries no pattern at all. Justice does not reveal hidden mysteries; it works in front of the curtain, with what can be seen, stated and weighed, and leaves the rest honestly unknown.

cards.name: The curtain behind the seat
cards.seen: Behind the figure hangs a pale blue lapis curtain gathered in swags beneath the shelf, its side lengths falling to cords that end in tassels level with the figure’s elbows.
cards.meaning: The curtain is Olivia’s own staging; the traditional card sets the figure against a plain ground. A curtain frames and also hides. Behind the display of plenty something is kept private, which leaves room to ask what the pleased surface covers, and whether anything behind it needs attention.

cards.name: The unlit Gothic window
cards.seen: A tall pointed arch frames tracery shaped as a bare, leafless tree rising from a single trunk, with the pentacles held in its branches. No light shows through, and pale snow lines the sill.
cards.meaning: In the traditional image the window glows, so the figures pass warmth they do not notice. Olivia’s window is dark, which shifts the question: support may be built into the world around you without being obvious from outside. The winter branches still carry the pentacles: dormant, not dead.

cards.name: The two lapis pillars
cards.seen: Two slender columns of lighter, mottled lapis stand at the left and right edges on the grassy bank, each with a plain capital and base, framing the figure, the pool and the star between them.
cards.meaning: Paired pillars stand on The High Priestess and The Hierophant; the traditional Star kneels in open country. Olivia’s pair turns the landscape into a threshold, and the figure kneels between them. Renewal is set at a doorway: a passage back toward life rather than a place to stay.

cards.name: The arch in the hedge
cards.seen: A low, dense hedge of textured lapis crosses the foreground; at its centre it rises into a rounded arch wreathed with small carved roses, and the path passes through its opening.
cards.meaning: The hedge arch is a traditional threshold between the tended garden and the wider world. It marks the moment of stepping out with what you have been given, from safe cultivation into practical use, through an opening that is narrow but clearly there.

cards.name: The lapis garden wall
cards.seen: A low wall of squared lapis blocks, paler and brighter blue than the sky, runs the full width of the card behind the horse, its top edge close to the child’s shoulders.
cards.meaning: The wall is commonly read as the edge of an enclosed garden: the child has come out beyond sheltered ground into open light. It can also suggest the safety that makes openness possible, a structure at your back rather than a barrier ahead.

name: Towers and houses
title: What is built, defended and left behind.
introduction: Buildings in tarot carry an old double sense. Medieval and Renaissance imagery made the tower a sign of both strength and pride: Saint Barbara holds one as her emblem, while the Tower of Babel stood for building too high. The Marseille pattern names its trump La Maison Dieu, the House of God, and shows its top struck off by fire from the sky; the Golden Dawn later linked the card to Mars. When the Waite-Smith deck of 1909 gave every Minor Arcana card a full scene, castles, towns and cottages filled its horizons, and readers commonly take them as what has been built: home, security, institutions, the life that goes on beyond the figure. Olivia carves every wall on this trail in lapis, often paler than the night sky and never in gold, so shelter reads as part of the setting, not as the prize. As you follow it, notice where each building stands: ahead, behind, overhead or broken.
comparison: On the Ace of Wands the castle is small and far off on a hill, a goal not yet built. The Four of Wands sets round crenellated towers behind the garland, a backdrop for the dance. On the King of Pentacles the castle rises from the King’s shoulders. The Four of Pentacles puts a walled city across an empty plain, behind the figure’s back. The Tower keeps its fitted lapis walls standing while its top breaks, an image of symbolic change, not a forecast. The Chariot faces away from domes and walls on both sides. On the Five of Cups a castle stands intact beyond the river, and the Ten of Cups ends at a small thatched cottage inside the arch.
prompt: Which structure in your life are you building, defending or ready to leave behind, and which one still stands?

cards.name: Castle on the hill
cards.seen: Far off on the left, a castle of pointed towers and turrets crowns a hill, carved in pale grey-blue lapis in the same low relief as the hills and trees around it.
cards.meaning: A castle on a distant hill belongs to the traditional image too, often read as the goal: the lasting structure a spark could one day build. It stays small and far away, because the Ace holds the beginning, not the finished stronghold.

cards.name: The castle behind the canopy
cards.seen: Beyond the garland rises a walled castle carved low in greyish-blue lapis: round crenellated towers, some with pointed roofs, and in front, a small gabled house with an arched doorway beside an arched bridge.
cards.meaning: In the traditional image a castle stands behind the celebrants, the settled place the festivity belongs to. Here it sits back in pale stone, not gold: security as the backdrop that makes celebration possible, not the prize itself. The Four is homecoming as much as achievement.

cards.name: The lapis castle
cards.seen: A castle carved in greyed lapis fills the space behind the throne: crenellated walls, conical-roofed towers and small arched windows rise from the King’s shoulders to well above the laurel wreath.
cards.meaning: In the suit of Pentacles a castle stands for what has been built and secured over time: property, institutions, a household that outlasts one season. The traditional image sets it in the distance; here it rises directly behind the throne, so the achievement backs the King up.

cards.name: The walled city behind
cards.seen: Carved in paler lapis on the horizon, a walled city of crowded roofs and pointed towers rises to one tall keep with a conical roof; crenellated walls and an arched gate face the plain, a low hill to the left.
cards.meaning: The traditional card sets a city behind the seated figure: the settled, built world of trade and shelter that security makes possible. Here it lies far off across an empty plain, and the figure sits with its back to it, which sharpens the question of what all the holding is for.

cards.name: The lapis tower
cards.seen: A tall tower of fitted lapis blocks rises on the right, topped with battlements. Its walls are carved stone by stone, and a dark arched opening sits low on its wall, half hidden by rock.
cards.meaning: The tower is the classic image of any structure built to protect or impress: a belief, a role, a way of arranging life. It is often compared with the Tower of Babel. Here, as in the traditional image, the walls still stand; what breaks is the top, which keeps attention on what was placed above the foundations.

cards.name: The walled city behind
cards.seen: Behind the columns, domed buildings, towers and walls are carved in paler lapis on both sides, with hills beyond. On the left a broad road curves out from the city in a long bend towards the chariot.
cards.meaning: In the traditional image a walled city stands behind the Chariot: the settled life the traveller has left, or the ground already won. Here it lies behind on both sides, so the card faces forward, away from everything familiar, along the curving way out.

cards.name: The castle on the hill
cards.seen: On a rocky hill at the right, beyond the river, stands a castle carved in paler lapis: a tall crenellated keep between round towers, one with a pointed roof, and arched doorways at its base.
cards.meaning: The traditional image places a building beyond the river, commonly read as home, shelter or the life that goes on. Here it is a full castle of several towers on its own hill, sturdy and intact above the water: a structure of safety the loss has not touched, still standing while the feeling takes its time.

cards.name: The cottage in the valley
cards.seen: Inside the arch, a small cottage with a thick thatched roof, a single chimney and a few dark windows sits on a low rise, carved in muted blue lapis among rolling hills.
cards.meaning: The house is the card’s quiet goal: home as a place of belonging rather than property. It sits far off and small, which keeps the image honest. The family does not stand inside the ideal; it looks toward it from open ground, where everyday life happens.

name: Crowns and wreaths
title: A crown is given; a wreath is won.
introduction: Tarot took its crowns from the Italian courts where it began. In the Marseille pattern the Emperor and the Empress are crowned, the Pope wears the triple tiara, and crowns recur through the court cards. The wreath comes from antiquity: laurel crowned the victors of the Pythian games and Roman generals in triumph, and from the Marseille pattern on, an oval garland surrounds the dancer of The World. In the kabbalah the Golden Dawn taught, the summit of the Tree of Life is Kether, the Crown, and the Waite-Smith deck of 1909 set laurel on the head and the staff of its victorious rider in the Six of Wands. In readings a crown usually speaks of authority held, a wreath of something achieved. Olivia carves these crowns and wreaths in ivory or lapis, touches one with a single gold sprig, and keeps the fullest gold for The World’s wreath. Notice what each is made of, and who placed it there.
comparison: The Emperor wears an ivory crown of upright points, set level on his head: an office worn. On The Tower a pointed lapis crown tips off the battlements where the bolt strikes: certainty unseated, symbolic change rather than a forecast. In the Two of Wands the crown turns to laurel: two lapis branches arch over the figure, their tips close but not joined. In the Six of Wands a ring of silvery laurel rises on the rider’s staff, one gold sprig tied where ring meets staff. The King of Pentacles wears laurel in place of a crown, and in The World a tall oval of gold laurel, bound with crossed ribbons, encloses the dancer.
prompt: Where in your life are you wearing a crown that came with a role, and where a wreath you earned?

cards.name: The ivory crown
cards.seen: An ivory crown of upright points, the tallest at the top centre ending in a small ball, sits level on the Emperor’s head. Long wavy hair falls from beneath it to the shoulders.
cards.meaning: A crown marks an office rather than a person: a responsibility held for as long as it is carried. Carved in the same ivory as the face and robe, not in gold, it reads here as a role the figure wears, not a treasure put on display.

cards.name: The crown knocked askew
cards.seen: At the summit a pointed crown of grey-blue lapis tips sideways off the battlements where the bolt hits it. Beside it, a cracked, crenellated fragment of the tower’s top breaks away to the right.
cards.meaning: The crown lifted off the tower is a traditional detail, commonly read as authority or certainty placed on top of a structure rather than built into it. Here the crown is stone, not gold: it looked like sovereignty but was made of the same material as the walls.

cards.name: Two arching laurel branches
cards.seen: Two leafy branches carved in pale grey-blue lapis rise on either side of the scene and bend inward over it, their tips drawing close above the figure’s head without joining.
cards.meaning: Laurel has long crowned victors and poets, and it is not part of the traditional Two of Wands. Olivia sets it as an unfinished arch: recognition is sketched around the figure but not closed. At this stage success is imagined, not yet won.

cards.name: The wreath on the staff
cards.seen: At the top of the rider’s staff an open ring of pale, silvery laurel leaves rises against the night. A small sprig of gold leaves is tied where the ring meets the staff, on its left.
cards.meaning: The wreath on the staff is the card’s classic sign of victory: the prize lifted where everyone can see it. Olivia adds a single sprig of gold, the only gold in the carving, so the eye lands on one precious point of worth inside the public display.

cards.name: The laurel wreath
cards.seen: In place of a crown, a wreath of pointed ivory laurel leaves circles the King’s head above long wavy hair; the calm face looks straight out at the viewer.
cards.meaning: Laurel was the classical wreath of victory and honour, given for something accomplished. The traditional King of Pentacles wears a crown; Olivia’s King wears a wreath instead, so the authority reads as earned through work rather than inherited, recognition rather than rank.

cards.name: The bound laurel wreath
cards.seen: A tall oval of gold laurel leaves encloses the dancer. At the top and again at the bottom, the two branches meet under a gold ribbon binding whose bands cross in a clear X.
cards.meaning: The oval wreath is the card’s oldest element, a victor’s crown made large enough to live inside. The Waite-Smith wreath is tied with red ribbons; here the bindings are gold and crossed, recalling the ancient form of Tau, the card’s Hebrew letter, once written as a simple cross mark.

name: Throne and scales
title: Power held, given and weighed.
introduction: The seat and the sceptre are among tarot’s oldest images. The hand-painted Italian decks of the fifteenth century already give the Emperor and Empress the regalia of rule, and Justice a sword and scales, the familiar emblems of that cardinal virtue in medieval and Renaissance allegory. In the Marseille pattern both rulers hold sceptres topped with an orb and cross, the globus cruciger of European monarchy. The Waite-Smith deck of 1909, following Golden Dawn teaching, numbers Justice eleven, and its Six of Pentacles shows the giver holding scales, so that weighing becomes part of generosity. In readings these objects tend to ask how power is held: gripped, built, rested in, carried lightly or measured out. Olivia carves the seats in ivory or lapis and keeps gold for very few objects, most tellingly the pans of Justice’s scales. As you follow the trail, watch the hands: what they hold, and how tightly.
comparison: On the Four of Pentacles the seat is a rough ivory block, square and plain, its surface pitted and unornamented. The Emperor turns the same square into architecture: a lapis throne with a panelled back, niched pillars and a stepped base. The Empress softens it into an ivory couch with deep cushions. The King of Cups keeps a throne but grips only a short ivory sceptre ending in a lotus bud. In the Two of Wands power becomes a small ivory globe cradled from beneath. The Six of Pentacles raises a pair of scales at shoulder height, empty pans on a beam close to level, and Justice pinches the balance by its ivory handle: gold chains, gold pans, both at the same height.
prompt: Where does your power sit today: on a block you will not leave, in a sceptre held lightly, or in an even scale?

cards.name: The squared ivory block
cards.seen: The figure sits on a plain rectangular block of rough ivory, visible on both sides of the robe, with squared edges and a pitted, unornamented surface; the robe falls over its front to the ground.
cards.meaning: The traditional figure sits on a simple block or stool rather than a throne. The cube is a classic image of Earth and of the number four: square, four-sided, hard to move. Olivia leaves it rough and plain, so the seat of this power is solid but unadorned, built for staying put.

cards.name: The block-built lapis throne
cards.seen: The throne is carved from paler, veined lapis as a set of square blocks: a tall panelled back, armrest pillars with blind arched niches and a carved frieze, all standing on a broad, stepped base.
cards.meaning: The traditional throne is a squared block of grey stone, and four, the Emperor’s number, is the number of the square. Olivia builds it like architecture, from right angles and arches: structure made visible, stable and lasting, and, when overdone, hard to move.

cards.name: The cushioned couch
cards.seen: The Empress reclines on an ivory couch with deep cushions, a scrolled arm at each end, a lattice-carved base and a turned leg, set on a low platform of lapis paving stones.
