cards.meaning: Where the Emperor sits upright on a stone throne, the Empress is traditionally shown on soft cushions in the open air. Olivia makes the seat almost a daybed: rest is not a pause from this power but part of it, the stillness in which things are allowed to ripen.

cards.name: The lotus-topped sceptre
cards.seen: The other hand grips a short, slender ivory sceptre near its lower end; the shaft rises to a small collar and ends in a carved flower head of layered, pointed petals, like a lotus bud.
cards.meaning: A short sceptre in the left hand is traditional for this King: authority used lightly. Olivia crowns it with a lotus, the flower that roots in mud and opens on water, and the Golden Dawn’s Prince of Cups also holds a lotus. Leadership here grows out of depth.

cards.name: The small ivory globe
cards.seen: At chest height one hand cradles a smooth ivory globe from beneath, fingers curled around its lower curve. Faint incised lines of coastlines and continents run across its surface.
cards.meaning: The globe is this card’s traditional emblem of reach: the whole world made small enough to hold. It stands for a plan rather than a territory. Resting in the palm while the real landscape lies behind, it asks whether you are studying the map or the ground.

cards.name: The raised balance scales
cards.seen: The giver’s left hand holds a pair of scales by the top of its upright pointer, at shoulder height; two shallow, empty ivory pans hang on cords from a beam that is close to level.
cards.meaning: The scales belong to the traditional design and are the key to the card: generosity that is measured, fair and proportionate. The pans here are empty, so the weighing is not of coins but of judgement itself: what is needed, what can be given, and on what terms.

cards.name: The gold-pan scales
cards.seen: The figure’s left hand, at the viewer’s right, pinches the ivory handle of a balance. From the knobbed ivory beam, three gold chains hang to each gold pan, and both pans sit at the same height.
cards.meaning: Scales are the oldest emblem of justice, weighing claim against claim, cause against effect. Gold is rare in this deck, and on the figure it appears only in the pans and chains: the act of weighing is what the card treasures most. The pans hang empty and even, ready, not yet decided.

name: Veiled sight
title: What stays hidden until you look.
introduction: The Marseille Hermit is already a cowled elder with a lantern, dressed like a monk or pilgrim. Blindfolds came from allegorical art: medieval sculptors bound the eyes of Synagoga, and Renaissance images blindfolded Cupid, Fortune and, later, Justice. The Marseille pips of Swords show only blades; the blindfolded Two and Eight familiar today come from the Waite-Smith deck of 1909, made by two members of the Golden Dawn. Pamela Colman Smith drew one figure seated with crossed swords and another bound among eight, and dressed the Five of Cups mourner in a black cloak. In reading, a hood or blindfold rarely means deceit; it marks attention held back: from a decision, from grief, from a crowd, or from a view not yet taken in. Olivia carves every hood and cloak here in ivory against the lapis night, and lays one blindfold in gold. At each card, ask whether the covering is chosen, imposed or ready to fall.
comparison: The Two of Swords wraps a flat ivory band across a calm, level face: sight set aside for now. On the Eight of Swords the band turns to gold and the head bows. The Five of Cups draws its hood forward over a mourner bent low, and in the Five of Pentacles a greyer hood shadows a face turned down to the snow, away from the gold star. The Six of Swords bows its hood over a child whose face looks out. The Eight of Cups shows only a hooded back, climbing. The Hermit bows a hooded head, eyes cast down past the outstretched hand, and the Three of Wands lets the hood rest at the neck of a figure facing the sea.
prompt: What are you choosing not to look at yet, and what would help you lift the covering a little?

cards.name: The ivory blindfold
cards.seen: A broad band of ivory is wrapped flat across the seated figure’s eyes. Long wavy hair, parted in the centre, falls to the shoulders; the mouth is closed and the face is level and calm.
cards.meaning: The blindfold is the card’s best-known sign: sight withheld, often read as a choice not to look yet. Here the face beneath it is composed rather than troubled, so the covered eyes suggest deliberate inward attention as much as avoidance: a mind turning away from outside noise to weigh something.

cards.name: The gold blindfold
cards.seen: A wide band of textured gold covers the eyes and wraps around the head, set into the ivory like gold leaf. The head bows forward and a little to the viewer’s left; the mouth is calm.
cards.meaning: The blindfold is this card’s oldest sign of limited sight: the situation is judged from inside, without the full view. Traditional versions use plain cloth. Olivia makes it gold, so what blocks the view is also something valued, a belief worth examining gently rather than tearing away.

cards.name: The bowed ivory hood
cards.seen: A tall figure carved in warm ivory stands wrapped from head to ground in one heavy cloak. The hood is drawn far forward over the face, and the head bends low toward the right.
cards.meaning: The traditional mourner wears black; Olivia’s is pale ivory, the brightest thing on the card. Grief here is not darkness but the most visible, most human presence in the scene. The hood turns attention inward: a time to feel rather than to be seen or to explain.

cards.name: The bowed, hooded head
cards.seen: Behind, on the left, a second figure in greyer, weathered ivory hunches forward under a deep hood, face shadowed and turned down towards the snow, a torn cloak trailing from the shoulders.
cards.meaning: The traditional image gives this walker injury and a hard road through snow. Here the hood and the lowered gaze matter most: neither figure looks up, so the gold star and the window go unseen. Hardship narrows attention to the next step, which is natural and also limiting.

cards.name: The hooded passenger and child
cards.seen: In the middle of the boat a seated figure, wrapped from head to knee in a hooded mantle, bows over a curly-haired child and holds the child close with both arms. The child’s face turns towards the viewer.
cards.meaning: The traditional card shows a huddled, cloaked passenger with a small child, often read as sorrow carried quietly and something tender protected on the way. Olivia’s passenger shelters rather than slumps: the bowed head reads as care, and the child’s face stays turned outward, towards the world beyond the boat.

cards.name: The hooded ivory traveller
cards.seen: The only ivory figure on the card walks away from the viewer, up a rocky path. A hood covers the head and a heavy cloak falls in deep folds to the ankles. The feet are bare, one heel lifted mid-step.
cards.meaning: The departing figure is the heart of the traditional image: someone leaving what they have built. Olivia’s traveller is hooded and barefoot, closer to a pilgrim than a wanderer. We never see the face, so the card asks you to supply the reason for leaving yourself.

cards.name: The lowered, hooded head
cards.seen: The ivory figure is shown in profile facing left, hood drawn well forward, a long wavy beard falling onto the chest. The eyes are cast downward past the outstretched hand, not up at the stars.
cards.meaning: The hood is the traditional sign of withdrawal: attention pulled in from the crowd so it can be spent on one thing. The beard marks the figure as an elder, whose authority comes from long looking. The lowered gaze makes wisdom a matter of where the next step goes.

cards.name: The figure seen from behind
cards.seen: An ivory figure with short curled hair stands with its back to the viewer, wrapped in a long, heavy cloak with a hood gathered at the neck; the hem falls to the feet on the rock.
cards.meaning: The turned back is the card’s classic gesture: attention given wholly to what lies ahead. It invites you to stand where the figure stands rather than meet its gaze. The plain, weighty cloak suggests patience and readiness for a long watch rather than display.

name: The open hand
title: What is given, held and let go.
introduction: Early Christian and medieval artists, reluctant to picture God directly, often showed only a hand reaching out of a cloud, the Dextera Domini, to bless, to crown or to give. Tarot kept that hand. Marseille-pattern decks set a hand from a cloud on the Aces of Wands and Swords; in the Golden Dawn lineage it appears on all four Aces, as in the 1909 deck Pamela Colman Smith drew for A. E. Waite, so that every suit begins as something offered. Other cards carry gestures older than tarot: two fingers raised in blessing, palms turned up to receive, fists closed to keep. In reading practice a hand shows how a card relates to its gift: taken, clutched, shared or released. Olivia carves these hands in ivory against lapis and keeps gold for what passes between them: a star on a disc, a heart on a cup. As you follow them, watch whether the fingers open or close.
comparison: In the Ace of Pentacles a large palm reaches from the cloud and holds the disc without closing over it. In the Ten of Wands both hands clutch the bundle to the chest. Strength holds another way: one hand flat on the mane, the other’s fingers resting between the jaws without strain. The Hierophant lifts two fingers with the palm turned out, a hand that speaks rather than takes. In the Two of Cups two hands reach, a thin band of lapis still between the fingertips. In the Six of Cups the kneeling figure opens both palms beneath the goblet, not yet touching it. The Six of Pentacles ends with a giver’s hand that has already let go.
prompt: What are your hands doing at present with what you have been given: holding it out, holding on, or letting it go?

cards.name: The open palm
cards.seen: A large ivory hand, palm upward, reaches in from the right with its wrist bare; the fingers extend relaxed past the disc’s left edge, and nothing closes over the disc, which rests on the palm ungripped.
cards.meaning: Every Ace shows a hand from the clouds: something given that you did not make yourself. In Pentacles the hand offers rather than wields. Because it holds the disc open and loose, the gift is not yet anyone’s possession; it waits to be taken up and used.

cards.name: Two clutching hands
cards.seen: One hand grips the bundle just below the chin; the other, a closed fist on a bent arm, holds it lower against the chest. Below the grip, the lower ends of the staves splay out towards the viewer’s left.
cards.meaning: The staves are hugged, not balanced on a shoulder or tied with a cord. This is a load carried by holding on, which takes both hands and leaves none free. The splaying ends suggest a bundle that is already slipping from its own arrangement.

cards.name: Hands on head and jaw
cards.seen: One ivory hand rests flat on the crown of the lion’s mane. The other slips its relaxed, slightly curled fingers between the lion’s open jaws, without any visible strain in the wrist or arm.
cards.meaning: Waite’s description has the figure closing the lion’s jaws, and readers have long debated whether the jaws are being closed or opened. Olivia leaves the question open: the hands neither force nor pry. One steadies, the other is trusted. The strength shown is contact, not pressure.

cards.name: The hand raised in blessing
cards.seen: The figure’s right hand, on your left, lifts to shoulder height, palm turned outward, index and middle fingers raised straight while the others fold down. The sleeve falls back from the wrist in heavy ivory folds.
cards.meaning: This is the old sign of blessing and teaching from Christian art, and the traditional Hierophant makes the same gesture. It is a hand that speaks rather than seizes: authority offered outward, on behalf of something larger than the one who raises it.

cards.name: Hands almost meeting
cards.seen: At the centre of the lower card the two free hands reach toward each other: one extended with fingers pointing forward, the other open with the palm showing. A thin band of lapis still separates the fingertips.
cards.meaning: The gesture is an offer and a response, not a grasp: one hand reaching, one ready to receive. This is Olivia’s own emphasis. The small gap matters: it keeps the moment one of choice, where either person can close the distance and nothing is taken for granted.

cards.name: Open hands below
cards.seen: The kneeling figure lifts both hands just beneath the goblet, palms up and fingers spread, not yet touching it, while the face tilts upward toward the taller figure.
cards.meaning: Open, upturned palms are the classic gesture of receiving. The small gap between hands and cup holds the moment in suspense: the gift is offered, not taken. It draws attention to the part of you that still knows how to receive simply, without bargaining or suspicion.

cards.name: The giver’s lowered hand
cards.seen: The giver’s right hand reaches down and outwards from a wide sleeve with an embroidered cuff, fingers pointing down and loosely curled, directly above the gold pentacle; the giver’s gaze is lowered towards it.
cards.meaning: In the traditional image coins drop from the giver’s hand into waiting palms. Here the hand has already let go and stays open and relaxed, neither grasping nor pushing. It shows giving as release: the gift leaves the giver’s control the moment it is offered.

name: The heart
title: A heart pierced, kept, then raised.
introduction: The pierced heart is older than tarot reading. Late medieval devotion showed the Virgin of Sorrows with swords in her breast, and the Sola Busca deck of about 1490 already sets a heart run through by three blades on its Three of Swords, an image Pamela Colman Smith took up for the Waite-Smith deck of 1909. The Marseille card has none. Waite-Smith adds one more: a heart-shaped shield bearing Venus’s sign beside The Empress. Cups, the Golden Dawn’s suit of Water, came to stand for feeling, and cartomancers paired them with playing-card hearts. Olivia carves the heart three ways: once as an anatomical organ in ivory, once as a lapis shield bearing Venus’s sign in gold, and six times as a small gold heart inlaid on a cup. Gold is rare in this deck, so each gold heart marks what is precious. Follow it and notice who holds it, and whether it is wounded, kept close or raised.
comparison: The Three of Swords carves a real ivory organ, three blades meeting inside, gold seams like mended cracks: a picture of hurt, not a forecast. On the Five of Cups a gold heart marks a goblet on a ledge, in the direction the bowed head turns, still unseen. The Queen of Cups keeps hers on a lidded vessel, turned towards you but closed. The Two of Cups holds it low at the waist. The Empress sets hers down: a lapis shield with Venus’s sign against the couch. The Three of Cups raises it high, the Nine of Cups lifts it to the peak of the arc, and the Ten of Cups sets it at the keystone of the arch.
prompt: Where is your heart resting today: pierced, kept in a closed vessel, held low at the waist, or raised with others?

cards.name: The carved ivory heart
cards.seen: An anatomical heart carved in ivory, not a stylised valentine: the great vessels rise from its top, its chambers swell in soft relief, and all three blades meet inside it.
cards.meaning: In tarot the heart stands for feeling, attachment and whatever you hold dear. Pamela Colman Smith drew a flat red emblem; Olivia’s is a real organ, heavy and alive, so the hurt reads as something bodily and lived, not a symbol kept at a distance.

cards.name: The gold-hearted cup
cards.seen: On a flat rock ledge to the right, a little further back than the figure, a tall goblet stands upright. A small heart of gold is set between two incised bands on its bowl.
cards.meaning: In the traditional card two cups still stand behind the mourner, commonly read as what remains. Olivia marks one of them with gold, the deck’s sign of what is precious. It stands in the direction the figure faces, but the bowed head has not yet lifted to see it.

cards.name: The gold heart
cards.seen: A small heart of gold is set into the smooth upper band of the bowl, just below the lid and facing the viewer; apart from the flecks in the sky, it is the only gold on the card.
cards.meaning: The traditional card has no heart on the cup; this is Olivia’s own addition. It names what the closed vessel protects: love and care that are real and precious, kept safe rather than displayed. Gold, used sparingly in this deck, marks the heart as the point of value.

cards.name: The gold heart on the cup
cards.seen: The right-hand figure holds a stemmed goblet low at the waist, fingers curled beneath the bowl. Set into the ivory bowl is a heart of glittering gold, the only gold on the card besides the star flecks.
cards.meaning: The heart does not appear on the traditional card. Gold in this deck is rare and marks what is precious. Placing it on one cup, held quietly at the waist and not yet offered, suggests that the most valuable feeling in a meeting is often the one still being held, waiting for a safe moment.

cards.name: The heart with Venus’s sign
cards.seen: Leaning against the side of the couch is a heart-shaped shield of paler grey-blue lapis with a raised rim, bearing the circle-and-cross sign of Venus inlaid in gold.
cards.meaning: The Waite-Smith Empress rests a heart-shaped shield bearing the Venus symbol against the throne, naming the card’s planet. Olivia uses gold sparingly, and here it marks this sign: love, beauty and pleasure set down as a shield, protection that works through warmth rather than force.

cards.name: The gold heart
cards.seen: A small heart of inlaid gold sits on the bowl of the central cup; apart from the star flecks in the dark border, it is the only gold on the card and the brightest point at its centre.
cards.meaning: The traditional Three of Cups has no heart on it at all. Olivia marks the meeting point of the three cups with gold, the deck’s sparing sign of something precious: what is being raised here is shared feeling, the warmth that belongs to all three at once.

cards.name: Gold heart on the centre cup
cards.seen: The fifth cup, at the peak of the arc and directly above the figure’s head, carries a small inlaid heart of bright gold on its bowl. The other cups show only scattered, irregular gold flecks.
cards.meaning: The heart is Olivia’s addition; the traditional card marks no single cup. Placed at the top of the row and aligned with the smiling face, it suggests that among many satisfactions one matters most: the wish that is really your own, not the ones collected for show.

cards.name: The gold-heart cup
cards.seen: At the very top of the arch, directly above the cottage, one lapis goblet carries a solid gold heart inlaid across its bowl. Five cups descend the arch on either side of it.
cards.meaning: Cups are the suit of Water: feeling, love and relationship. Olivia sets a heart-marked cup at the keystone, where the traditional arc of ten cups has no single centre. Everything on the arch leans toward one warm point, as if the household’s feeling were gathered there.

name: The child
title: Small hands at every threshold.
introduction: Children entered tarot early. Some fifteenth-century Italian World cards show two putti holding up a globe, and on the Marseille Sun two children stand before a wall beneath the sun’s rays. Renaissance painters and carvers often used such small figures for love, play and plenty. The numbered Marseille Minor Arcana, though, show arranged suit signs rather than scenes; the children of the Six and Ten of Cups and the Ten of Pentacles belong to the illustrated Waite-Smith deck of 1909, which places a child inside memory, household joy and a family line. Readers commonly take the child as a beginning: openness before habit, trust before proof, and whatever one life hands on to the next. Olivia carves most of its children in ivory, like the adults beside them; on this trail one is pale grey-blue and one is lapis. As you follow them, notice what each child holds, where each stands beside the grown figures, and which way each one faces.
comparison: On Death the child is small and pale grey-blue, walking barefoot beneath the horse and holding up a flower in both hands. In the Six of Cups an ivory child kneels and looks up at a taller figure bending down. The Sun sets one child alone on the horse, riding bareback, one arm flung wide, palm open. Judgement turns the child away from you, arms raised in a wide V. On The World two small children dance on rocky ledges, each lifting a tiny gold wand. In the Ten of Cups two children dance hand in hand. The Ten of Pentacles ends in lapis: a child rests a hand on the head of a slender dog that faces left, towards the elder.
prompt: What was handed on to you when you were small, and what would you like to hand on in turn?

cards.name: The child with a flower
cards.seen: Beneath the horse’s belly, between its front and hind legs, a small barefoot child in a short tunic, carved in pale grey-blue, steps forward and holds up a small flower in both hands.
cards.meaning: A child is part of the traditional crowd around Death, commonly read as innocence that meets change without fear. Here the child is on foot beneath the horse, walking the same way it goes, and the small flower held up answers the rose on the banner above.

cards.name: The kneeling child
cards.seen: On the right a smaller ivory figure with long hair tied back kneels in a sleeveless gown with a draped sash, looking up toward the taller figure, who stands barefoot and bends down from the left.
cards.meaning: In the traditional image both children stand, one shorter than the other. Kneeling makes the difference in height the whole subject: one looks down with care, the other looks up with trust. The card is often linked with innocence and the inner child, the self who first learned what kindness feels like.

cards.name: The child with open arms
cards.seen: An ivory child sits bareback on the horse, a light ivory cloth hanging from the shoulders and gathered across the lap. One arm is flung wide with the palm open; the other hand grips the banner staff.
cards.meaning: The child is the Sun’s central image of trust: open to the light, unguarded, with nothing to prove. Where Marseille cards show two children beside a wall, the Waite-Smith card and Olivia’s carving focus on one child whose whole body turns outward in welcome.

cards.name: The child with raised arms
cards.seen: At the centre, a curly-haired child in a short ivory tunic stands with back to the viewer, both arms raised high in a wide V, fingers spread, bare feet planted on the floor of the coffin.
cards.meaning: The child seen from behind is a traditional detail, and it places you where the child stands: facing the call. Raised arms are the plainest answer to it, open and unguarded. The child is not stepping anywhere yet, only saying yes with the whole body.

cards.name: Two children with wands
cards.seen: Below the wreath two small ivory children, each trailing a ribbon of drapery, dance on rocky ledges either side of a winding river, and each holds up a tiny gold wand.
cards.meaning: The children are not part of the Waite-Smith pattern, though some fifteenth-century Italian World cards show two putti holding up a globe with a walled city inside. Echoing the dancer’s wands in miniature, they bring the completion above down into play in the ordinary world below.

cards.name: The dancing children
cards.seen: To the right, two smaller ivory children hold hands mid-dance, knees bent, heels lifted, each raising the free arm. The curly-haired one laughs openly; the taller, long-haired one tips the face upward.
cards.meaning: Children dancing in this card are traditionally read as joy that needs no reason, and as the future a household makes room for. In the traditional image the children play facing each other, turned away from the rainbow; here each lifts a free arm skyward, so their play and the adults’ wonder share one upward reach.

cards.name: The child and the dog
cards.seen: At the right, beside the arch’s right pillar, a curly-haired child in a tunic, carved in lapis, rests one hand on the head of a slender standing dog and raises the other; the dog faces left, towards the elder.
cards.meaning: A child reaching for a dog appears in the traditional card as the youngest generation, curious and unhurried. Here the child stands at the far side from the elder, and the dog turns back across the scene, a thread of attention running from youngest to oldest.

name: Angels and wings
title: Messengers between the sky and the ground.
introduction: The word angel comes from the Greek for messenger, and in medieval and Renaissance art a winged figure marked a meeting of heaven and earth. Marseille-pattern decks show a winged figure pouring between two vessels on Temperance and an angel sounding a trumpet over the rising dead on Judgement; on the Marseille Lovers the figure above is a Cupid with a bow, which the Waite-Smith deck turned into a great angel with open arms. Renaissance painters also recast the fearsome cherubim of the Bible as winged children’s heads, and in the Waite-Smith deck they are carved into several Queens’ thrones. In readings a winged figure often points to guidance, a wider view, or a call from beyond the scene. The Olivia deck carves most of its angels from the same grey-blue lapis as the night sky, while its cherubs appear in ivory or blue stone. Follow them from ornament to messenger, and notice how much sky each one fills.
comparison: In the Queen of Cups a plump winged cherub is carved in lapis on the throne’s lower panel, one arm reaching up the frame. The Queen of Pentacles lifts two into the rose vine beside the arch: one looks down, one turns its face towards you. In The Sun two ivory cherub heads float by the horse’s legs. Wheel of Fortune seats a winged figure on a cloud in a corner, bowed over an open book. In The Lovers the angel rises from lapis clouds, wings across most of the card’s width, hands open. Temperance is the angel: ivory wings from head to hip. Judgement ends with wings spread towards both upper corners, a hand at the mouthpiece, eyes lowered.
prompt: Which kind of guidance reaches you most easily at present: a small watcher close by, or a call from far above?

cards.name: Cherubs on the throne base
cards.seen: On the lower panel of the throne, carved in blue lapis, a plump winged cherub faces the viewer and reaches one arm up the frame, while a second small head peeps out behind it; leafy scrolls fill the panel.
cards.meaning: The small childlike figures on this Queen’s throne are commonly read as undines, spirits of water, and as the playful, imaginative side of feeling. Olivia carves them as cherubs that echo the winged handles of the cup, so tenderness appears in the seat as well as in the Queen’s hands.

cards.name: Two winged cherubs
cards.seen: Two cherub heads with small feathered wings nestle in the rose vine, one on each side of the arch; the left one looks down, the right one turns its round face out towards the viewer.
cards.meaning: In Pamela Colman Smith’s design, cherubs are carved into the throne itself, a sign of love and innocence held within material comfort. Here they have moved up into the living roses, so tenderness sits inside the growing world, not only in its furniture.

cards.name: Two winged cherub heads
cards.seen: Level with the horse’s legs, two ivory cherub heads with small feathered wings and draped collars float against the lapis, one in front of the forelegs and one under the belly, between fore and hind legs.
cards.meaning: Cherub heads do not appear on the Waite-Smith card; they come from Renaissance art, where they mark a scene as blessed. Some early Italian Sun cards show a winged child holding up the sun. Here they suggest joy that is shared and quietly watched over.

cards.name: The reading angel
cards.seen: In the upper left corner a winged figure is seated on a cloud, head bowed over an open book held in both hands. It is carved in the grey-blue of the lapis itself, not in ivory.
cards.meaning: The four winged creatures come from Ezekiel’s vision and the Book of Revelation, and later stood for the four evangelists. Among the fixed signs the human face is linked with Aquarius. Here, as in the traditional image, the creature reads: steadiness found in study while the wheel turns below.

cards.name: The angel above the clouds
cards.seen: A large winged figure carved in grey-blue lapis, not ivory, rises from a bank of lapis clouds. The wings spread across most of the card’s width; the arms open wide with both hands held open.
cards.meaning: Later readers often name this angel Raphael, the angel of healing, and read it as a blessing or a wider view over the relationship. Here it is cut from the same stone as the night sky rather than the couple’s ivory: guidance woven into the landscape, not a third person standing in the scene.

cards.name: The raised ivory wings
cards.seen: Two large ivory wings rise behind the shoulders, their upper curves level with the head and their long flight feathers falling to about hip height, carved feather by feather against the blue ground.
cards.meaning: Temperance is traditionally drawn as an angel, a go-between linking what is above with what is below. The traditional wings are often coloured red; Olivia keeps them the same ivory as the robe, so the whole being reads as one calm, even substance with nothing flaring or urgent.

cards.name: The trumpeting angel
cards.seen: Carved in pale grey-blue lapis rather than ivory, the angel leans out of the clouds with wings spread towards both upper corners, head bowed, eyes lowered, one hand at the mouthpiece and the other lower on the shaft.
cards.meaning: The angel of Judgement is commonly identified as Gabriel, the messenger whose call wakes the sleeping. Olivia carves it from the same blue stone as the night rather than from ivory, so the call reads as part of the sky itself, sounded with lowered eyes towards the figures below.

name: The lion
title: The wild, held in an open hand.
introduction: The lion entered tarot as a virtue. Some early painted decks show Fortitude as a Hercules-like man raising a club over a lion; the Marseille pattern settles on a woman calmly holding its jaws. Saint Mark’s lion, one of the four creatures of Ezekiel and Revelation, holds a corner of the Marseille World. In the nineteenth century Eliphas Lévi gave the Chariot two sphinxes in place of horses, and the Golden Dawn tied Strength to Leo; the Waite-Smith deck of 1909 set lions on the Wands thrones and a black cat at the Queen’s feet. In readings the great cat stands for courage, appetite and instinct; what matters is how they are held. Olivia carves most lions in lapis, the stone of the night, so the wild belongs to the landscape; ivory is kept for a sphinx, a cat and a resting lion. Follow them from a lion met hand to jaw to one keeping a corner of the whole.
comparison: In Strength the lapis lion lifts its open mouth to the figure: the wild met, not beaten. The Chariot’s ivory and lapis sphinxes face opposite ways, held by no reins, only by the figure above. On the Queen of Wands a pale cat sits upright by the Queen’s foot: instinct kept close. The King of Wands turns two lion heads outward like guardians. In the Two of Cups a winged lion’s head hovers above the couple. The Four of Swords lays an ivory lion at the sleeping knight’s feet; on the Wheel of Fortune a sphinx reclines, a sword across its forelegs. In The World a maned lion rests its forepaws on a cloud, one fixed corner of the whole.
prompt: Where is your own lion right now: met hand to jaw, pulling two ways, sitting quietly at your feet, or keeping watch?

cards.name: The lapis lion
cards.seen: The lion is carved in greyish-blue lapis, not ivory, with a deep wavy mane. Its forepaws are planted, its open-mouthed head lifted to the figure, and its tail sweeps out to the right, curling up at the tip.
cards.meaning: The lion is Leo, fire, appetite, pride and raw vitality: everything strong that can also overwhelm. Cut from the same stone as the night and the hills, it belongs to the landscape rather than opposing it. Its lifted face and loosely curling tail read as trust, not defeat.

cards.name: The ivory sphinx
cards.seen: On the left, an ivory sphinx lies with forepaws stretched out and tail curled round its haunch, a small wing carved on its shoulder and a wreath in its hair. Its face turns outward, left.
cards.meaning: Eliphas Lévi replaced the Chariot’s horses with two sphinxes, one light and one dark, and the Waite-Smith card kept them. The light sphinx is commonly read as one of two opposing drives: here it looks firmly away from its partner, towards its own side.

cards.name: The pale seated cat
cards.seen: An ivory cat sits upright at the front of the dais beside the Queen’s visible foot, eyes open and facing the viewer, its tail curled forward along the step.
cards.meaning: The black cat of the traditional Queen of Wands is commonly read as intuition, independence and ease with what is hidden. Olivia carves the cat in the same pale ivory as the Queen, so the instinct it stands for looks less secret: self-possession that is simply part of the figure, calm and awake.

cards.name: Lion heads on the throne
cards.seen: Two lion heads carved in greyed lapis sit on the top corners of the throne back, manes thick, facing away from each other, joined by a scrolling crest that rises to a central palmette.
cards.meaning: The lion is Leo’s animal and the classic image of fire carried with dignity; the traditional King of Wands also has lions on the throne. Turned outwards like guardians, they set the tone of the card: courage that watches over a territory rather than prowling for a fight.

cards.name: The winged lion’s head
cards.seen: At the top of the central staff a lion’s head with open jaws and a full mane spreads two broad feathered wings, carved in the same pale greyish blue lapis as the distant hills.
cards.meaning: Pamela Colman Smith also crowned this card with a winged lion’s head. The lion is commonly read as fire, desire and courage; the wings lift that heat toward something higher. Attraction is present here, but it hovers above the couple, shared rather than owned by either.

cards.name: The lion at the feet
cards.seen: At the right end of the slab a small maned ivory lion lies with forepaws stretched out and head turned toward the viewer, the effigy’s pointed armoured feet resting just above it.
cards.meaning: The traditional tarot image has no lion. On medieval tombs a lion at the feet commonly stood for courage and steadfastness. Olivia adds it as a quiet guardian: strength does not vanish during rest, it lies down and keeps watch.

cards.name: The sphinx and sword
cards.seen: An ivory sphinx with a striped headdress and a raised feathered wing lies along the top of the wheel, forepaws on the rim, a cross-hilted sword laid across its forelegs, point to the right.
cards.meaning: In the Waite-Smith card a seated sphinx holding an upright sword crowns the wheel, commonly read as the still point of judgement above constant motion. Olivia’s sphinx reclines, calm rather than alert: the part of you that can watch a change without being spun by it.

cards.name: The lion on the clouds
cards.seen: At lower left a heavily maned lion in grey-blue lapis rests its forepaws on a cloud beside the wreath, head in three-quarter view and turned towards the centre, above a rocky river valley.
cards.meaning: The lion stands for Mark and for Leo, fixed Fire: courage and warmth held steady. In the Waite-Smith card the lion sits at lower right and the bull at lower left; Olivia has them change places, so the lion keeps watch on the side of the raised wand.

name: The horse
title: From the charge to the free rein.
introduction: The horse is tarot’s image of energy that can be carried. Renaissance Italian decks already set each suit’s Knight on horseback, and medieval art, following the pale horse of the Book of Revelation, often showed Death riding. The Tarot de Marseille keeps horses for its Knights and The Chariot. The Waite-Smith deck, shaped within the Golden Dawn lineage, puts a white horse under Death, under the child of The Sun and under the victor of the Six of Wands, and gives each Knight’s horse its own pace. Readers commonly take the horse as vitality and drive, and the rider as the will that guides it. On this trail Olivia carves four horses in ivory, two in the same lapis as the land around them and one in both stones; none is gilded. As you follow it, watch the legs slow from leap to standstill across the four Knights, then watch the rein loosen until no hand holds it.
comparison: The Knight of Swords’ horse charges, mouth open around the bit and both forelegs off the ground, ivory to the chest and lapis from the shoulder. The Knight of Wands’ horse is caught mid-leap, hind hooves planted, front end in the air. The Knight of Cups slows to a walk on a greyer lapis horse, head bowed, one foreleg lifted by the water. The Knight of Pentacles’ horse stands in mottled lapis, all four hooves on the furrows. In the Six of Wands an ivory horse steps high, reins in the rider’s one lowered hand. Death’s pale horse walks evenly on a slack rein. The Sun’s horse stands saddleless, its rein held by neither hand: strength that needs no steering.
prompt: What energy in your life are you still holding on a tight rein, and what might it carry if you loosened your grip?

cards.name: Horse of ivory and lapis
cards.seen: The horse’s head, neck, mane and chest are ivory; from the shoulder the stone turns to blue lapis for body, legs and tail. Its mouth is open around the bit, both forelegs bent and lifted clear of the ground.
cards.meaning: The horse carries the knight’s force and mirrors the rider’s temper. Here ivory is kept for the upper parts of horse and rider, and everything below turns to lapis, as if the thinking part leads while the rest still belongs to the night it rushes through.

cards.name: Forelegs in mid-leap
cards.seen: Both forelegs are lifted clear of the ground and folded at the knee, hooves hanging; the hind legs stretch back and down, hooves planted beside tufts of dry scrub.
cards.meaning: Waite noted that the motion of the horse is a key to the rider’s character. This is the moment of take-off: weight thrown onto the haunches, front end already in the air. It is the card’s whole temperament in one gesture, committed before the landing is known.

cards.name: The blue horse, head lowered
cards.seen: Carved in lighter, greyer lapis rather than ivory, the horse bows its head deeply, mane cut in flowing strands; a bridle crosses its face and a broad rein patterned with leafy scrolls runs back to the rider’s low hand.
cards.meaning: Waite noted that this Knight rides quietly, and the horse carries that mood. Here it is made of the same stone as the river and hills, as if the landscape of feeling itself were carrying the rider. Its bowed head reads as gentleness and patience, not charge.

cards.name: The heavy, standing horse
cards.seen: A thick-necked, broad-bodied horse carved in mottled lapis stands side-on facing left, ears pricked; all four hooves rest flat on the furrows and its long tail hangs straight down.
cards.meaning: The other knights of the tradition ride out, even the Knight of Cups at a walk; this horse is traditionally heavy and still. Olivia keeps it planted and carves it in the same lapis as field and sky, so its strength seems drawn from the land it stands on.

cards.name: The white horse
cards.seen: An ivory horse, larger than any walker, carries the rider to the right. Its neck arches, a bridle and reins run to the rider’s lowered hand, and the front leg at the far right is lifted high.
cards.meaning: The white horse is traditional for this card: strength, momentum and a pure, clear success. Its raised foreleg shows a parade step, energy under control. The rider holds the reins lightly with one hand, guiding power rather than fighting it.

cards.name: The pale walking horse
cards.seen: A large ivory horse walks towards the left at an even pace, the near foreleg lifted. The bridle is plain, the rein runs in a slack curve from the bit up to the rider’s hands, and the eye is calm.
cards.meaning: A white horse is traditionally a carrier of purity and strength, and here it walks rather than charges. The loose rein matters: nothing is being driven or forced. Change in this card moves at the pace of a steady walk, which is why it cannot be hurried or outrun.

cards.name: The white horse
cards.seen: A large ivory horse stands calmly facing left, all four hooves on the grassy ground. It wears a simple bridle but no saddle, and a slack rein runs back to the child’s waist, held by neither hand.
cards.meaning: A white horse is commonly read as strength that is willing and well directed. The child rides without a saddle and without holding the rein, so the card points to energy that cooperates with you instead of needing to be forced or steered.

name: Birds and butterflies
title: From the swallow’s flight to the eagle’s view.
introduction: Winged creatures have carried meaning in tarot since its early printed decks. The Marseille Star shows a small bird perched in a tree beside the kneeling figure, and the Marseille World gives the eagle of John the Evangelist one corner among the four living creatures. Christian art gave the dove to the Holy Spirit, and the Greek word psyche meant both soul and butterfly. In the Golden Dawn system Swords belong to Air, and in 1909 Pamela Colman Smith filled that suit’s court cards with birds and butterflies; on her Ace of Cups a dove descends with a wafer. Readers commonly take birds as thought, news and spirit, and butterflies as change. In the Olivia deck most of these creatures are cut into the lapis, pale grey-blue against the night; a few are raised in ivory, and gold appears only on the Queen of Swords’ crown. As you follow them, notice which fly free, which rest and which are held.
comparison: The order moves from flight through stillness to the widest view. In The Fool two lapis swallows glide between low bands of cloud. In the Ace of Cups an ivory dove dives head first, a round wafer in its beak. Above the Page of Swords pale birds scatter in a loose trail. In The Star a long-legged bird, commonly read as an ibis, stands on its branch facing the stars. In the Nine of Pentacles a hooded ivory falcon perches on a gloved hand. On the Queen of Swords’ throne butterflies are scattered behind her head; on the King of Swords’ they sit in mirrored pairs. In The World a lapis eagle lifts its wings on a bank of cloud.
prompt: Which winged creature is closest to your mind today: the swallow setting out, the falcon that waits, or the eagle that sees the whole?

cards.name: Two swallows among clouds
cards.seen: Two small birds with long, pointed wings glide through the upper left of the sky between low bands of cloud. They are carved in the pale grey-blue of the lapis itself, not in ivory.
cards.meaning: Swallows do not appear in the Waite-Smith Fool; they are Olivia’s addition. They return with spring, and sailors wore them as emblems of homecoming, so they add a seasonal kind of beginning: travel that is also, in some way, a return.

cards.name: The dove with the wafer
cards.seen: An ivory dove dives head first beneath the column, wings spread wide, holding a small round wafer in its beak just above the cup; a thin glassy stream runs from beneath the wafer into the bowl.
cards.meaning: The descending dove with a wafer is a signature detail of Pamela Colman Smith’s 1909 Ace of Cups, drawn from Christian images of the Holy Spirit and the Eucharist. It speaks of grace: feeling that arrives as a gift, not an achievement. The traditional wafer bears a small cross; Olivia’s is plain.

cards.name: The scattered birds
cards.seen: Small pale birds with outstretched wings, carved in light lapis, fly in a loose trail across the sky above the trees on the left, with a few more on the right near the horizon.
cards.meaning: Birds belong to air and are commonly read as messages, news and thoughts in flight; a flock is traditional on this card. Scattered rather than in formation, they suggest ideas and information arriving from several directions at once, not yet gathered into one clear message.

cards.name: The ibis in the tree
cards.seen: At the upper right a leafy tree, carved in pale grey-blue lapis, rises from a small hill. A long-legged bird with a long down-curved beak stands on one branch, facing left toward the stars.
cards.meaning: The bird in the tree is commonly read as an ibis, sacred to Thoth, the Egyptian god of writing and measure: thought at rest while the body works. It is carved in the same muted blue as the tree and stays in the background. Insight can wait on its branch until the pouring is done.

cards.name: The hooded falcon
cards.seen: An ivory falcon perches on the raised hand at left, talons gripping a fitted glove with a flared cuff. A small hood with a loop on top covers its head; its long tail hangs down beside the wrist.
cards.meaning: The hooded falcon is the card’s best-known emblem: a wild, swift creature trained to wait and to return. It is commonly read as discipline turned into freedom, instinct brought under calm control. The figure’s eyes are lowered elsewhere; the bird no longer needs watching.

cards.name: Butterflies on the throne
cards.seen: Several butterflies of different sizes are carved in shallow relief on the tall lapis throne back, scattered behind the Queen’s crown, head and shoulders; another rests on the side panel below the armrest.
cards.meaning: Repeated from crown to throne, butterflies make transformation the ground this Queen sits on, not only an ornament worn. Carved in the same greyed blue as the throne rather than gold, they are the quieter, settled form of the change the crown celebrates.

cards.name: Six lapis butterflies
cards.seen: Six butterflies carved in pale grey-blue lapis are arranged in mirrored pairs inside the wreath: two beside the upper crescent, two larger ones level with the King’s head, and two small ones lower down.
cards.meaning: Butterflies are carved on the traditional throne of this King and recur on the Queen’s: creatures of air, commonly read as the soul, breath and transformation. Set here in symmetrical pairs, they suggest a mind that has changed through experience and now holds those changes in order.

cards.name: The eagle with lifted wings
cards.seen: In the top right corner a large lapis eagle perches on a bank of cloud, both wings lifted and half open, its hooked beak turned left towards the centre of the card.
cards.meaning: The eagle is linked with John and, in the Golden Dawn lineage, with Scorpio, fixed Water. Its raised wings give this corner height: feeling that has risen above its own depths and can take in the whole scene below.

name: The circle
title: Loops that close and open again.
introduction: The circle is the plainest shape of return. Medieval and Renaissance imagery set Fortune beside a turning wheel, with figures rising on one side and falling on the other, and the tarot trump kept that picture; in the Marseille pattern half-animal figures ride a wheel turned by a crank. Alchemical manuscripts drew the ouroboros, a serpent biting its own tail, for what ends and begins again. The Waite-Smith lineage, shaped by the Golden Dawn, made these signs explicit: a lemniscate over the Magician and over Strength, a serpent belt on the Magician, a wheel written over with letters and alchemical symbols. Readers commonly take them as continuity, exchange and renewal. Olivia sets the lemniscates and the wheel in gold, a metal it spends sparingly, and carves the other loops in ivory or lapis. As you follow the trail, notice whether each loop is closed or open, still or turning, held close to the body or set free in the sky.
comparison: On the Two of Swords a medallion of concentric rings rests on the breast, the sword shafts converging toward it: the circle as a still centre. The Magician opens it into a gold lemniscate of two closed loops. Strength lifts the same figure into the night sky. The Two of Pentacles loosens it into an ivory ribbon of open loops, swinging from one disc to the other. In the Two of Cups the line doubles into two serpents twining around a staff, heads raised to face each other. On the Page of Swords spirals are incised into boulders like ancient carvings. The Wheel of Fortune ends with a bare gold wheel of eight spokes, a circle built to turn.
prompt: Which cycle in your life keeps bringing you back to the same place, and what is different about you each time you return?

cards.name: The medallion over the heart
cards.seen: A round raised disc sits on the breast of the gown, its lower edge meeting the crossed wrists, its face carved with concentric rings. The two sword shafts converge toward it.
cards.meaning: This medallion is not part of the traditional image; it is Olivia’s own detail. A circle is wholeness and a still centre. Placed at the point where both blades meet, it suggests that the two options are held from one place, and that the heart is present even while the mind keeps the choice open.

cards.name: The gold lemniscate
cards.seen: Above the head floats a horizontal figure of eight inlaid in gold, two smooth closed loops crossing at the centre. It is the largest piece of gold on the card, set against the pale blue field behind the figure.
cards.meaning: Pamela Colman Smith drew a lemniscate over the Magician and again over the figure in Strength, and Olivia keeps both in gold. The sign of infinity is commonly read as endless exchange: energy flowing out and returning. In a deck sparing with gold, it marks what does not run out: attention, renewed each time it is given.

cards.name: The gold lemniscate
cards.seen: A figure-eight lying on its side, inlaid in textured gold, floats in the upper centre of the night sky, well above the figure’s bowed head and brighter than any star around it.
cards.meaning: The lemniscate also crowns the Magician, and is commonly read as endless, self-renewing energy. The traditional image sets it just over the figure’s head; Olivia lifts it high into the sky, so the steadiness it stands for seems to reach the scene from above rather than belonging to anyone.

cards.name: The looping ribbon
cards.seen: A long, flat ivory ribbon loops up behind the raised pentacle, crosses the lifted forearm, swings out behind the back to the left of the body and curls down beside the lower disc, making several open loops against the sky.
cards.meaning: The cord joining the two pentacles in the traditional image is commonly read as the lemniscate, infinity laid on its side: endless exchange between two demands. Here it is looser, several loops rather than a neat figure eight, which suits a balance that is improvised rather than fixed.

cards.name: Twin serpents on the staff
cards.seen: Two serpents wind around each other and around a straight staff beneath the lion, then raise their heads at the same height to face each other just under the wings.
cards.meaning: This is the caduceus, the herald’s staff of Hermes, messenger and go-between, not the single-serpent rod of healing. Two forces twine without either winning, and the heads meet level: a picture of communication, negotiation and balance, the conditions in which two people can truly meet.

cards.name: Spirals in the stone
cards.seen: Two concentric spirals are incised into the boulders at the lower left, like ancient rock carvings; the lower one is larger, with more turns, and the upper sits on a rounded stone.
cards.meaning: Spirals are not part of the traditional Page of Swords; they are Olivia’s addition. An ancient carved motif, often read as growth that comes back to the same point at a new level, they sit well beneath a student whose thinking is still circling towards clarity.

cards.name: The bare gold wheel
cards.seen: A large gold wheel fills the centre: a heavy outer rim around a band of paler lapis, an inner ring over a darker field, and a small ringed hub with a raised boss, joined by eight gold spokes.
cards.meaning: The traditional wheel is written over with letters and alchemical signs; here it is left bare, with no inscription to decode. Gold is used sparingly in this deck, so the turning itself is what is precious: the cycle as a real force, not a riddle to solve.

name: The wand
title: From living branch to heavy armful.
introduction: Before it was a wand it was a club. Italian decks call the suit Bastoni, the Tarot de Marseille Bâtons: cut staves or cudgels, drawn on the numbered cards as interlaced bars with no scene. The Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn assigned Wands to Fire in the late nineteenth century, and Pamela Colman Smith, drawing the Waite-Smith deck of 1909, turned the bars into living wood that still puts out leaves and gave every number its own scene. Readers have since followed the suit as a story of will and drive: spark, plan, structure, contest, load. Olivia carves many of its wands in ivory like the figures, cuts others into the lapis ground, and saves gold for the few points where a leaf or flame breaks out. Begin with the Magician’s raised wand, then follow the staff from Ace to Ten: notice who holds it, how many there are, and whether they grow, stand or weigh down.
comparison: The Magician raises one slender ivory rod high above the head. On the Ace of Wands a single ivory staff, knotted like a cut branch, sprouts leaves above and below the fist. The Two of Wands carves it in grey-blue lapis, its tip opening in gilded leaves. The Four of Wands plants four lapis wands, vines twisting up every shaft. The Five of Wands multiplies smooth ivory staves until at least seven tips cross above the heads. The Eight of Wands releases eight ivory wands in parallel flight. In the Nine of Wands twelve blue staves stand six on either side of the figure, and the Ten of Wands gathers ivory staves into one armful fanned over a bowed head.
prompt: Which of these wands looks most like your own drive right now: raised, sprouting, planted, crossing others, in flight, or carried as a load?

cards.name: The raised ivory wand
cards.seen: The figure’s right arm, on the viewer’s left, reaches up and out above the head, the fingers closed around a slender ivory rod held nearly upright, with a small grooved knob at its top end.
cards.meaning: The raised wand is the first half of the Magician’s gesture, commonly read as “as above, so below”: energy drawn from above in order to be brought down into form. It is a conductor rather than a weapon; held this high, it makes an intention visible before anything is made.

cards.name: The living staff
cards.seen: A straight ivory staff, knotted like a cut branch and blunt at its lower end, rises from the hand to the bud; small sprigs of serrated leaves grow from it above and below the fist.
cards.meaning: In decks that follow Pamela Colman Smith’s design the wands of this suit are living wood that still sprouts, commonly read as will, desire and creative force. Fresh shoots on a cut stick say the impulse is organic: it grows when tended, not when forced.

cards.name: The gold-budded wand
cards.seen: The taller wand, on the right, is a knotted staff of grey-blue lapis with small side shoots. At its tip a bud opens in gilded leaves, the only gold beyond the scattered stars.
cards.meaning: Wands are the suit of Fire: will, desire and creative drive, and a leafing staff is that fire still growing. Of the two wands, only the one in the figure’s grip has begun to open, and in gold. The live energy is in what you are actually holding.

cards.name: Four living wands
cards.seen: Four slender wands carved in blue lapis relief stand planted in the ground, two on each side of the dancers. Carved vines twist up every shaft, and each tip breaks into sprouting leaves against the night.
cards.meaning: Wands are the suit of Fire: will, drive and creative spark. In the traditional image four budding staves hold up a garland. Olivia winds each one with carved vine and lets its tip branch into leaves, so the structure built by effort stays alive rather than finished and fixed.

cards.name: The crossing staves
cards.seen: Long, smooth ivory staves cross and recross above the heads, pointing every way at once. At least seven separate upper tips can be counted against the sky, more than the five of the title.
cards.meaning: The traditional image gives each of five youths a single wand. Olivia multiplies them until it is hard to tell whose staff is whose. That is the texture of the Five: energy everywhere, crossing rather than aligned. Crossed staves can be a clash, or the frame of something being built together.

cards.name: Eight wands in parallel flight
cards.seen: Eight ivory wands, each with a rounded bud-like head and a slimmer knobbed foot, slant together across the lapis sky from upper right to lower left, closely spaced and parallel, none crossing another.
cards.meaning: Wands are the suit of Fire: will, energy and creative intent. Eight moving in one direction make the card’s whole statement, many efforts travelling at once and in agreement. No figure holds or throws them here; the effort has already been released and is under way.

cards.name: Twelve blue staves
cards.seen: Twelve knotted staves carved in the blue lapis itself, each with cut branch stubs, stand upright on the rim of the oval ground, six on either side of the figure, some nearer to us and some behind.
cards.meaning: Pamela Colman Smith’s 1909 card lines eight wands up behind the figure like a fence. Olivia sets twelve, more than the title’s nine, in a broken ring on both sides of the figure. That is the card’s double edge: a palisade protects, and it can also enclose the one who keeps it.

cards.name: The fanned ivory wands
cards.seen: Long ivory staves rise from the figure’s grip and fan out above and beyond the bowed head against the night sky. Eight rough tips are clearly visible, each shaft knotted with small cut-off twig stubs.
cards.meaning: Wands belong to Fire: drive, purpose and the energy to begin things. Ten of them together is every plan and commitment gathered into one armful. Their fan rises high over the bowed head and leans in the direction of travel, so the load stands taller than its carrier.

name: The cup
title: From one chalice to an arch of ten.
introduction: Cups are among the oldest suit signs in the pack: Italian playing cards took them from Mamluk cards by the late fourteenth century. The Marseille pattern set them out as ornate vessels arranged by number, with a towering, architectural cup on the Ace. In the Golden Dawn system Cups belong to Water, and when Pamela Colman Smith painted a scene into every pip for A. E. Waite in 1909, the cup became a story: visited by a dove, raised in a toast, ignored, spilled, lined up and left, strung along a rainbow. Readers take it as feeling, love, imagination and what nourishes you. The Olivia deck carves it in two materials: ivory in human hands, grey-blue lapis when it stands in the landscape or is offered from a cloud. Gold is rare and chosen: an eight-pointed star, a small heart. As you follow the suit, notice who holds the cup and where the gold falls.
comparison: In the Ace of Cups one hand holds a wide ivory chalice upright. In the Three of Cups three ivory goblets meet above the dancers’ heads, a gold heart on the central bowl. The Four of Cups offers a star-marked lapis cup from a cloud, while the seated figure looks down at the grass. In the Five of Cups three goblets lie on their sides, two of them trickling. The Six of Cups offers a plain ivory goblet in both hands, a gold heart on its bowl. The Eight of Cups leaves eight unbroken cups in two rows. The Nine of Cups sets nine out in an arc, and the Ten of Cups carves ten star-marked goblets along an arch.
prompt: Where is your cup today: held open, raised with others, overlooked, spilled, offered, or set out in a full row?

cards.name: The ivory chalice
cards.seen: A wide, deep ivory chalice with a moulded rim, a carved knop on its stem and a broad lobed foot decorated in low relief, held upright at the centre of the card.
cards.meaning: The cup is the emblem of the suit of Water: a vessel for feeling, love, intuition and imagination. At the Ace it is a single open container, not yet shared or spilt. It suggests capacity: an inner space that can receive and hold what arrives.

cards.name: Three raised cups
cards.seen: Three ivory goblets on short knopped stems meet above the heads of the dancers, each held up by a single hand; the central one is larger and set slightly higher, the two outer cups close on either side.
cards.meaning: Cups are the suit of Water: feeling, love and relationship. Raised together they make a toast, the old gesture of pledging one another. Here the three bowls almost touch, so the image reads less as three separate drinks than as one shared celebration.

cards.name: The star-marked fourth cup
cards.seen: Held out in mid-air at the upper right, a stemmed cup of grey-blue lapis carries a small gold star with eight slender points on its bowl, the only gold set into any cup on the card.
cards.meaning: In the traditional image the fourth cup is plain, a gift from outside that the figure does not see. Olivia marks it with the same eight-pointed gold star that shines on the Ace of Cups: what is offered here is a fresh beginning of feeling, not simply one more of the same.

cards.name: Three fallen cups
cards.seen: Three pale grey lapis goblets lie on their sides, one to the left of the figure and two in the foreground, their bowls carved with round, coiled ornament. Thin pale trickles run from the mouths of two of them.
cards.meaning: Three spilled cups are the heart of the traditional image: what has been lost, and what cannot be poured back. Here they are carved as finely as the cups still standing, a reminder that grief measures value; what has gone mattered because it was worth carrying.

cards.name: The gold-hearted cup
cards.seen: The standing figure bends forward and offers a plain ivory goblet with a rounded bowl, short stem and wide foot, holding it in both hands; a gold heart is inlaid on the front of the bowl.
cards.meaning: In the traditional card the cups brim with white flowers. Here the offered goblet holds no visible flowers at all, only a heart of gold: the gift is the feeling itself. It is the only gold on the figures, marking simple kindness as the treasure of the scene.

cards.name: Eight cups in two rows
cards.seen: Eight stemmed cups, three in the upper row and five in the lower, are carved from the same blue lapis as the ground. All stand upright and unbroken, rims level, lined up close together.
cards.meaning: Cups hold feeling, relationship and what nourishes you. Nothing here is spilled, unlike the Five of Cups. These are real achievements, neatly arranged; carved from the landscape itself, they read as something established. The card’s question is why something so orderly no longer satisfies.

cards.name: Nine cups in an arc
cards.seen: Nine stemmed goblets stand in a shallow arc along a curved ledge, each carved from grey-blue lapis with a fluted lower bowl and a rounded knop on the stem. The row dips lower toward both ends.
cards.meaning: Nine is the fullest number before the Ten, and the arc of cups is traditionally read as emotional abundance on display: everything wished for, gathered and set out. Carved from the same blue stone as the sky, these cups belong to the scene rather than glittering apart from it.

cards.name: Ten star-marked goblets
cards.seen: Ten grey-blue goblets with knopped stems and fluted feet are carved in low relief along the arch, five either side of the heart cup. Each bowl bears a tiny incised star touched with gold.
cards.meaning: The traditional card shows ten cups riding a rainbow. Counting the heart cup, Olivia’s arch holds eleven: ten star-marked cups keep the card’s number, and the extra one reads like a heart held in common. Their small stars echo the night sky around them.

name: The sword
title: The blade lowered, laid down, then raised upright.
introduction: The sword entered European cards with the first packs of the late fourteenth century, one of four suits inherited from Mamluk playing cards. Medieval and Renaissance allegory already gave it meaning: Justice held a sword beside the scales, and the Marseille Justice still does. The Marseille pips weave curved blades into an oval, while their Ace raises one straight sword through a crown. The Golden Dawn tied Swords to Air, the element of thought, speech and judgement, and Pamela Colman Smith’s scenes for the Waite-Smith deck of 1909 turned each number into a moment: grief, rest, defeat, a crossing. In readings the blade is clarity that can also wound. Olivia carves most blades in ivory; as the suit darkens, more are cut from lapis and held by no one, and gold touches a Page’s hilt and a Knight’s blade. As you follow it, notice who holds the sword, and which way its point faces.
comparison: On the Ace of Swords the ivory blade hangs point down from a hand in a cloud, aimed at mountains and travellers. The Three of Swords drives its centre sword straight into a carved heart: a picture of hurt, not a forecast. The Four of Swords lays three lapis swords flat on a chapel wall, held by no one. The Five of Swords hugs two blades to the chest, owned but not used. The Six of Swords carries six upright across the water. The Eight of Swords plants lapis blades beside and behind a figure, none in front. The Ten of Swords sets nine in a row along a back, with no blood. Justice raises one ivory blade upright again.
prompt: Which sword are you holding at the moment: one aimed at real ground, one hugged as proof, one carried across, or one held upright?

cards.name: The blade pointing down
cards.seen: Below a three-lobed pommel and a crossguard whose ends curl into round scrolls, the long ivory blade hangs point downward, a fine central ridge running to its sharp tip above the mountains.
cards.meaning: Swords belong to Air: thought, speech and the power to tell one thing from another. The traditional Ace raises its blade point upward into a crown. Olivia turns it toward the earth, the mountains and the travellers, so this clarity is aimed at lived ground: an idea brought down to where it can be used.

cards.name: The upright centre sword
cards.seen: The central ivory sword stands exactly vertical, its flared, fluted pommel and bound grip high among the clouds, its crossguard ending in rounded knobs, its blade driving straight down into the heart.
cards.meaning: Swords belong to Air: thought, words and clear understanding. The straight middle blade is the plain fact of what happened, the one line that does not bend. Its symmetry keeps the image from chaos; the pain has a clear axis you can name.

cards.name: Three swords on the wall
cards.seen: Three lapis swords lie horizontally one above another across the back wall, points to the left, hilts to the right with disc pommels and straight crossguards; the lowest is set furthest right.
cards.meaning: In the traditional image three swords hang point down above the sleeper, the troubles of the Three of Swords hung up for now. Olivia lays them flat and level, which reads even more like a truce: the weapons are stored, not threatening, and nobody is holding them.

cards.name: Two swords hugged close
cards.seen: Two ivory swords are clasped diagonally against the chest by one crossed arm, blades rising past the shoulder to just above the horizon, hilts low on the chest at the viewer’s left: one crossguard and two round pommels.
cards.meaning: Swords belong to Air: thought, argument, the words you choose. Two blades hugged to the body suggest arguments collected and kept as proof. The grip is possessive rather than ready; these swords are not being used, only owned, and that is the card’s question about victory.

cards.name: Six upright ivory swords
cards.seen: Six ivory swords stand in a close row in the left half of the boat, points hidden inside the hull, hilts rising above the passengers: knobbed pommels, straight crossguards, plain blades, the row fanning slightly apart.
cards.meaning: Swords are the suit of Air: thoughts, words and decisions. In the traditional image they ride upright in the boat, and here too nothing is thrown overboard. What was learned in difficulty comes along; standing clear of the passengers, the blades are carried, not wielded.

cards.name: Five blades on the right
cards.seen: Five more swords of the same dark lapis stand on the viewer’s right against the rocky slope, at staggered heights. Nine blades in all flank the figure; none touches it, and none stands in front.
cards.meaning: The traditional card shows eight swords, matching its number. Olivia’s carving shows nine, while this deck’s Nine of Swords carves eight, as if the two cards had traded counts. What matters more is the open ground: every blade stands behind or beside the figure, and the way forward is clear.

cards.name: Nine lapis swords
cards.seen: A close row of swords carved in greyish blue lapis, not ivory, stands upright above the figure’s back. Counted carefully there are nine, each with a round ball pommel, a straight crossguard and a groove down the blade.
cards.meaning: The traditional card shows ten blades, the full count of the suit, and swords stand for thought, words and judgement. Olivia’s image shows nine on a card named Ten. One way to read the gap: the last blade is missing because this is the point where the adding finally stops.

cards.name: The upright ivory sword
cards.seen: Raised in the figure’s right hand, at the viewer’s left, a straight double-edged blade points upwards, its tip rising just above the crown. The fist closes just below a straight crossguard; a round pommel shows beneath it.
cards.meaning: The sword is discernment: the power to cut cleanly between what is true and what is merely comfortable. Held upright rather than swung, it is ready, not attacking. Its double edge is commonly read as a reminder that honest judgement cuts both ways, including towards the one who holds it.

name: The pentacle
title: A gold star from open palm to hem.
introduction: The pentacle began as a coin. Italian and Marseille-pattern decks call the suit Coins: round discs set among stylised foliage, with the Ace drawn as a single large ornamented coin. The Golden Dawn called the suit Pentacles and tied it to the element of earth, and the Waite-Smith deck of 1909 carried that name into wide use. Pamela Colman Smith drew a five-pointed star within each disc and gave most numbered cards a scene: a sculptor at work in a church, a worker beside a bush of discs, a family beneath an archway. In reading practice the pentacle stands for what is tangible: body, money, work, home, time. Olivia cuts the disc in ivory or in lapis and keeps gold for very few stars, often a single one on a card. Follow that gold as the suit counts upward, from one seed of value to what a household keeps and hands on.
comparison: On the Ace of Pentacles a plain ivory disc rests on an open palm, one small gold star near its centre: value as a seed. In the Three of Pentacles the gold star crowns the arch above two lapis outlines, a shared aim. The Four of Pentacles presses a large gold-starred disc against the chest. In the Six of Pentacles one gold-starred disc hangs between the giver’s hand and upturned palms. The Seven of Pentacles gilds only the bush’s highest disc. The Eight of Pentacles hangs seven finished discs on a pillar, stars in outline; its only gold lies on the bench, under the chisel. The Ten of Pentacles sets its gold low, near the hem of the elder’s robe.
prompt: Where in your life is value still a seed, and where is it ready to be held, shared or handed on?

cards.name: The ivory disc and gold star
cards.seen: A thick, plain ivory disc with a raised rim around a slightly recessed face rests on the open palm; near its centre sits one small five-pointed star of gold.
cards.meaning: The pentacle is the suit’s emblem of earth: coin, body, craft and the ground you stand on. The traditional image carries an interlaced pentagram; here the sign is pared to a solid gold star on bare ivory, a single point of value in a still unworked piece of material.

cards.name: The gold pentacle above
cards.seen: At the apex of the pointed arch, inside a moulded circle, a solid five-pointed star is inlaid in gold; it is the only gold on the carved architecture and sits above the other two.
cards.meaning: The pentacle is the suit’s emblem of earth: body, material, money, work made real. Setting the one gold star at the top of the triangle suggests a shared aim held above the individual contributions, the standard everyone is working towards rather than any one person’s share.

cards.name: The gold star on the disc
cards.seen: Pressed flat against the chest, a large plain ivory disc carries a five-pointed star inlaid in textured gold, the only large piece of gold on the card; elsewhere gold appears as small flecks and tiny stars in the sky.
cards.meaning: This is the pentacle held close and the heart of the card: what is valued most, guarded against the body. It is the only one of the four still framed by its disc and the only one in gold, as if all the worth were gathered into the thing being clasped while the rest fade to plain stone.

cards.name: The gold-starred pentacle
cards.seen: A sixth disc, paler grey-blue with a raised rim, carries a five-pointed star inlaid in gold; it hangs in the air between the giver’s hand and the upturned palms below.
cards.meaning: Gold is rare in this deck, and of the six pentacles only the one in motion carries it. The value is shown at the moment of exchange, not while it sits in the sky. What makes a resource precious, the carving suggests, is that it reaches someone who needs it.

cards.name: The gilded top pentacle
cards.seen: At the crown of the bush, higher than every other disc, one grey-blue pentacle carries a five-pointed star outlined and partly filled in gold; the six discs below it show only incised stars.
cards.meaning: The pentacle is the suit’s coin and seed: earth, body, resources and the value of work. Gilding only the highest disc is Olivia’s own touch. It reads as the result still ripening at the top of the plant, the part of the harvest that is visible and wished for but not yet within reach.

cards.name: Seven pentacles on the pillar
cards.seen: Seven finished ivory pentacles hang from small pegs down a square pillar of paler lapis beside the bench, five along its left edge and two staggered to the right; each star is cut in outline, not gold.
cards.meaning: Displayed work traditionally shows skill building up piece by piece, the pentacles made so far. The traditional image hangs them on a plain upright post; here they climb a stone pillar that rises above the horizon, so steady practice becomes something upright and lasting.

cards.name: The gold pentacle
cards.seen: Low against the robe, near the hem, a lapis disc bears a solid five-pointed star of worked gold, the only gilded emblem on the card; a grey disc with a line-drawn pentagram rests higher, against the elder’s lap.
cards.meaning: Gold is rare in Olivia’s deck and marks what matters. Of all eleven discs, only the one at the hem of the elder’s robe is golden, and its star is solid rather than drawn in line. It sits low, near the ground, as if what lasts is often humble and close at hand.
